issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## Description

In Iris multi-backend mode, each task backend owns its live worker inventory and
placement (which attempt runs on which worker). The in-process RPC backend keeps
this in a local store, and the design rule is: a backend's worker/placement store
is a **cache**, not durable truth. If a backend loses it, that is treated as "all
tasks were lost" — the controller's durable record (`task X is assigned/running on
backend Y`) re-routes the work through the normal reschedule path — never as a
fatal reconcile error.

The one thing blocking a fully store-free RPC backend is the worker reconcile
protocol. Today `ReconcileRequest.desired` is documented as the *complete expected
set*, and a worker stops any local attempt whose UID is absent from it
(`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py`, `lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/worker.proto`).
A backend that comes up with an empty placement store would therefore tell every
worker to stop everything before it could re-learn what is running.

Add an observe-before-converge (recovery) path to the worker reconcile protocol so
a freshly-started backend can learn the attempts a worker is running *without*
issuing stops, then re-adopt them. With that, the RPC backend's placement store
becomes a pure cache rebuildable from live worker reports + provider state, and the
backend can run with no durable local DB at all.

This overlaps the multi-backend recovery work (the level-triggered reconcile +
epoch fence, "PR4" of the program); file it so the store-free-backend endpoint is
tracked on its own.

### Definition of Done

- The worker reconcile protocol supports an observe-only / recovery phase: a backend
  learns running attempts from worker reports without those reports being read as a
  desired-set teardown.
- A backend that starts with an empty placement store re-adopts the attempts its
  workers report rather than stopping them.
- The in-process RPC backend can run with an ephemeral (non-durable) placement store.
- Covered by a restart test: wipe the backend's placement store mid-run; running
  attempts survive and are re-adopted.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 This is design-stage, multi-module work (proto change + worker reconcile + backend recovery + ephemeral store + restart test) that **overlaps the in-flight multi-backend "PR4" program** (design #6718; impl #6730, #6731). The RPC backend's placement store referenced in the DoD does not exist on `main` yet — it lands with those PRs. Per the agent scope rule (>100 LOC / multi-module / design), no PR; posting root cause + a proposed approach for a human to review and sequence against PR4.

# Research

The only thing forcing a backend to keep durable placement is the reconcile protocol's *complete-desired-set* semantics. `ReconcileRequest` carries `worker_id` + `desired` and nothing else; the worker treats any non-terminal local attempt whose UID is **absent** from `desired` as a zombie and kills it. A backend that restarts with an empty placement store sends an empty `desired` and tells every worker to stop everything before it can re-learn what is running.

**Relevant code**
- [`worker.proto#L73-L76`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/worker.proto#L73-L76) — `ReconcileRequest`, `desired` = "complete expected set"
- [`worker.py#L871-L881`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L871-L881) — zombie-kill: absent-from-`desired` ⇒ `_kill_async`
- [`worker.py#L889-L911`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L889-L911) — observations bounded to `desired` ∪ zombies (won't surface unknown-to-backend attempts)
- [`reconcile/worker.py#L110-L221`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/worker.py#L110-L221) — `build_reconcile_plans` builds `desired` from durable state
- [`controller/backend.py#L340-L363`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/backend.py#L340) — `TaskBackend` protocol (where the RPC backend + its placement store hangs)

The existing worker-side container adoption ([`worker.py#L319-L398`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L319-L398)) recovers attempts across a *worker* restart; this issue is the symmetric case for a *backend* restart, and needs a protocol affordance rather than local container scanning.

# Proposed Approach

**1. Add an observe-only phase to the reconcile protocol.** Add a field to `ReconcileRequest` — `bool observe_only = 3;` (or a `ReconcileMode mode` enum if more phases are foreseen). When set, the worker:
  - skips the zombie-kill loop ([`worker.py#L871-L881`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L871-L881)) — absence is *not* a stop signal;
  - still applies explicit `run`/`stop` intents (so a recovering backend can keep handing out specs);
  - reports its **complete** non-terminal attempt set in `observed`, not just the desired∩local subset ([`worker.py#L889-L911`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L889-L911)).

This makes the absent-UID case mean "I don't know yet," distinct from today's "stop this."

**2. Backend recovery (observe → adopt → converge).** A backend that comes up with an empty placement store runs an observe-only sweep across its workers, rebuilds placement from `observed` attempt UIDs cross-referenced with the controller's durable `task assigned/running on backend Y` record (and provider state), then flips to normal converge mode. Attempts the durable record disowns fall out through the existing reschedule path — never a fatal reconcile error.

**3. Ephemeral placement store.** Once placement is rebuildable from live worker reports + provider state, the in-process RPC backend's store becomes a pure cache and can be non-durable. This piece lands against the RPC backend introduced in #6730/#6731.

**4. Test.** Restart test: with attempts running, wipe the backend's placement store mid-run; assert running attempts are observed and re-adopted (not stopped) and that no `stop`/zombie-kill is issued during the observe phase. A focused worker-level test (`tests/cluster/worker/test_reconcile.py`) can assert that an `observe_only` reconcile with empty `desired` returns the full observed set and kills nothing.

**Sequencing question for a human:** steps 1–2 (protocol + worker semantics) are independent of the RPC-backend store and could land first as a small, self-contained proto+worker change with the worker-level test. Steps 3–4 should ride on PR4 (#6730/#6731) where the store exists. Recommend splitting along that line unless PR4 owners want it bundled.

issues.author: teetone
issues.body:
Goal: Investigate whether Self-Verified Distillation improves post-trained Marin checkpoints

Self-Verified Distillation generates candidate solutions from a post-trained model, filters them using verification, and trains on the accepted self-curated data. The goal of this issue is to evaluate whether this procedure further improves a post-trained Marin checkpoint using unlabeled seed questions. The original SVD paper studies this setting without external teachers or tool feedback, where the model generates candidate solutions, self-verifies them, and trains on the resulting filtered dataset.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26132

### Motivation

We want to test whether large post-trained Marin models can further self-improve through on-policy SVD. In the pure setting, the Marin checkpoint is used both as the generator and verifier.

A key risk is that the initial Marin checkpoint may be too weak, as either:

- a generator: producing too few high-quality candidate solutions
- a verifier: failing to reliably distinguish correct from incorrect generations

If self-verification is the bottleneck, we should also evaluate a variant that keeps Marin on-policy generation but uses a stronger verifier for filtering.

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Hold-one-feature-out ablations on the fast_track MoE rungs (d512, d768) to measure how much each
existing architectural/optimizer feature contributes, giving bearings before testing new features.

## Hypothesis or Goal

For each feature, drop it (holding everything else fixed) and compare Paloma/uncheatable bpb to the
fast_track MoE baseline at the same size and **equal data** (same token budget as the baseline:
d512 = 2,385 steps, d768 = 6,930 steps, batch 128, seq 4096). FLOPs may drift; data is held fixed.

## Ablations (each drops/changes ONE feature vs the MoE baseline)

1. drop XSA (exclusive self-attention)
2. drop attn gate (headwise sigmoid gate)
3. drop gated norm (GatedNorm -> plain RMSNorm)
4. drop latent MoE (latent_dim=None; experts ~2x wider)
5. full rope on local (drop half-rope on local layers)
6. drop sconv (all 3 sites)
7. drop MuonH (route all MuonH param groups to AdamH)
8. halve granularity (192 experts, top-4, 2x expert width)
9. halve sparsity (192 experts, top-8, same width)
10. drop GQA (KV heads = Q heads)

10 ablations x 2 sizes (d512, d768) = 20 runs, plus the existing fast_track MoE baseline for
reference. Runs on cw-us-east-02a, W&B tags h100/fasttrack/vocab-16k + an ablation tag.

## Status

Branch off the fast_track branch (PR #9287). Ablation toggles added via a single `--ablation <name>`
flag on the fast_track launcher.

## Links

* PR (fast_track variant): https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9287

## Original request

> follow agent.md and lets test some simple hold-one-feature-out ablations on the d512 and d768 moe
> rungs. features: drop xsa, drop attn gate, drop gated norm, drop latent_moe (size experts twice as
> big), drop half rope on local (go full rope on local instead), drop sconv on all 3 sites, drop MuonH
> (route all MuonH groups to AdamH), halve granularity (top 4 of 192 at double size experts), halve
> sparsity (top 8 of 192 instead of top 8 of 384), and drop GQA (full kv matching q). 10 experiments
> at 2 sizes = 20 runs. 1 issue, branch off fasttrack, run on cw-us-east-02a. data match on all.

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

comments.body:
🤖 ## Hold-one-feature-out ablation results (Paloma macro loss)

**TL;DR — MuonH is by far the most load-bearing feature (~1.6× effective compute). On a wall-clock (MFU-adjusted) basis, LatentMoE and coarse granularity flip to net wins even though they're quality-neutral, because they raise throughput.**

Each run removes one feature from the d512/d768 MoE baseline, **data-matched** to it. Metrics are Paloma **macro loss** (lower is better). Effective speedup = the compute (Sc) / wall-clock (Sw) advantage the feature buys, from the fitted MoE law `L = 1.2 + A·C^(−0.0842)`:
- **Sc (equal-tps)** = compute the ablation needs to reach the baseline's loss ÷ its own budget = `((L_abl−1.2)/(L_base−1.2))^(1/α)`. >1 ⇒ feature is worth keeping on quality.
- **Sw (MFU-adjusted)** = `Sc × tps_base/tps_abl` — folds in the throughput change from removing the feature. >1 ⇒ feature is worth keeping on wall-clock.

### Setup (shared)
- Baseline `fasttrack-moe-d512` / `-d768`: Paloma macro loss **3.156 / 2.872**.
- Data-match: 2,385 / 6,930 steps = 1.25B / 3.63B tokens; batch 128; seq 4096; tokenizer `hero-bpe-v16384` (16k); 8×H100.
- Baseline scale: active 20.8M / 60.6M, total 483M / 1420M, lm_head 8.4M / 12.6M, total FLOPs 3.5e17 / 2.3e18. Structure-changing ablations (drop_latent, halve_granularity, halve_sparsity, drop_gqa) shift params/FLOPs; the rest match baseline.
- Branch [`fasttrack-ablations`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fasttrack-ablations) @ `1a81f5f688`. Effective speedup uses the MoE fit (α=0.0842, L∞=1.2 imposed) — sensitive to both.

### Results (ordered most → least load-bearing by d512 Δloss)

| ablation | L d512 | Δloss | Sc | Sw | L d768 | Δloss | Sc | Sw |
|----------|-------:|------:|---:|---:|-------:|------:|---:|---:|
| **drop_muonh** (→ AdamH) | 3.2355 | **+0.0796** | **1.61** | **1.63** | 2.9200 | **+0.0476** | **1.40** | **1.32** |
| halve_sparsity (top-8/192) | 3.1911 | +0.0353 | 1.24 | 1.16 | 2.9062 | +0.0339 | 1.27 | 1.13 |
| drop_sconv | 3.1904 | +0.0346 | 1.23 | 1.25 | 2.8866 | +0.0142 | 1.11 | 1.00 |
| halve_granularity (top-4/192 2×) | 3.1681 | +0.0122 | 1.08 | **0.88** | 2.8854 | +0.0130 | 1.10 | **0.84** |
| drop_gated_norm | 3.1675 | +0.0116 | 1.07 | 1.03 | 2.8795 | +0.0072 | 1.05 | 0.98 |
| drop_attn_gate | 3.1673 | +0.0114 | 1.07 | 1.07 | 2.8749 | +0.0025 | 1.02 | 0.99 |
| full_rope_local (drop half-rope) | 3.1640 | +0.0081 | 1.05 | 1.10 | 2.8722 | −0.0001 | 1.00 | 0.98 |
| drop_xsa | 3.1601 | +0.0042 | 1.03 | 1.03 | 2.8709 | −0.0014 | 0.99 | 0.98 |
| drop_latent (param-matched) | 3.1539 | −0.0020 | 0.99 | **1.23** | 2.8717 | −0.0006 | 1.00 | **1.23** |
| drop_gqa (full KV = Q heads) | 3.1383 | −0.0176 | 0.90 | 0.94 | 2.8469 | −0.0254 | 0.83 | 0.87 |

### Findings
- **MuonH dominates** — ~1.6× (d512) / 1.4× (d768) effective compute, and slightly more on wall-clock (dropping it doesn't speed the step up). Clearly the top ingredient.
- **Sparsity (top-8/384) and SConv** are solidly positive (Sc ≈ 1.2). SConv's wall-clock value fades to ~1.0 at d768.
- **Coarse granularity is a net wall-clock win:** halving granularity costs only +0.012 loss but is much faster, so Sw = 0.88 / 0.84 (< 1) — fine granularity is *not* worth it on wall-clock at this scale.
- **LatentMoE is quality-neutral but a throughput feature:** Sc ≈ 1.0 yet Sw ≈ 1.23 both sizes — keeping it buys ~1.23× wall-clock via higher MFU.
- **GatedNorm / attn-gate / half-RoPE / XSA** are marginal (Sc ≈ 1.0–1.07, Sw ≈ 1.0), i.e. near break-even, several already ~neutral at d768.
- **GQA trades quality for KV efficiency, and loses here:** full KV lowers loss (Sc 0.90 / 0.83) and stays a wall-clock win (Sw 0.94 / 0.87 < 1) — GQA's throughput saving doesn't pay for its quality cost at these sizes.

### Notes
- `drop_latent` is the **param-matched** variant (`drop-latent-pm`); the non-param-matched one (experts 2× wide) is excluded as a capacity artifact and its d768 run crashed.

### W&B runs (`marin-community/marin_moe`)
drop_muonh [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-muonh-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-muonh-d768) · halve_sparsity [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-halve-sparsity-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-halve-sparsity-d768) · drop_sconv [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-sconv-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-sconv-d768) · halve_granularity [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-halve-granularity-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-halve-granularity-d768) · drop_gated_norm [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-gated-norm-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-gated-norm-d768) · drop_attn_gate [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-attn-gate-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-attn-gate-d768) · full_rope_local [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-full-rope-local-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-full-rope-local-d768) · drop_xsa [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-xsa-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-xsa-d768) · drop_latent_pm [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-latent-pm-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-latent-pm-d768) · drop_gqa [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-gqa-d512) [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ft-abl-drop-gqa-d768) · baseline [moe-d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fasttrack-moe-d512) [moe-d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fasttrack-moe-d768)

issues.title: Agent fast_track Experiment: hold-one-feature-out ablations (d512/d768 MoE)

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Decouple the attention/MLP FLOPs from the residual-stream width so that scaling the residual
stream out is cheap, then measure how Paloma macro loss varies as a function of residual-stream
size at **fixed** attention/MoE compute.

The MoE already projects the token down to a latent (½ width) for the experts. This experiment
mirrors that on the attention path: a learnable-RMS-norm latent down-projection before attention
input and a plain up-projection on the output (no norm, mirroring the MoE up-projection). With both
attention and MLP living in the fixed-size latent space, the only params/FLOPs that grow with the
residual stream are the embedding, lm_head, the four latent down/up projections, the router, the
shared experts, and the norms. Because the vocab is small (16k), FLOPs grow slowly with residual width.

## Method

- **New baseline** = current fast_track MoE + attention latent projection (down w/ learnable RMSNorm,
  up w/o norm), at the family width (d512 → latent 256, d768 → latent 384).
- **Residual-width sweep** (d512 family): residual ∈ {384, 512, 640, 768, 1024, 1536} (base −128, base,
  +128, +256, +512, +1024), holding latent dim and every attention/MoE param size fixed at the base.
- Repeat for the **d768 family**: residual ∈ {640, 768, 896, 1024, 1280, 1792}.
- Optimizer recipe (LR/β2/ε) and token budget are pinned to the family baseline so only residual
  width varies. Data-matched, batch 128, seq 4096, on cw-us-east-02a. No checkpoints; eval on.
- 12 runs total (6 per family). Report Paloma macro loss vs residual width, with a FLOPs table.

## Exact prompt

> follow agent.md and lets try a new idea. First for the new baseline, take the moe and add a latent
> projection with learnable rms norm before the attn layer input. So similar to how MoE projects down
> to half, project attn down to half. then same on the output side, but output side doesn't need a
> learnable rms norm (mirror moe). So run that. then lets take the d512, and update the residual
> stream to -128, +128, +256, +512. keeping the latent dim size and moe/attn param sizes all the same.
> then repeat this on the d768 one. So 10 runs in total. The main idea here is we want to decouple the
> attn and mlp flops from the size of the residual stream. which makes scaling out the residual stream
> cheap. So we want to see how model quality varies as a function of residual stream size. Since vocab
> size is small, flops as a function of residual stream is small. also do +1024. Include a table with
> flops for each.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 ## Launched: 12 runs on cw-us-east-02a (version 2026.09.20)

Branch [`fast_track_resid_latent_scan`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fast_track_resid_latent_scan) @ `1047ce9`.

**Architecture change** (`model.py`): `CausalSelfAttention` gains an optional latent projection mirroring
LatentMoE — a learnable-RMSNorm down-projection of the residual to `attn_latent_dim` before Q/K/V and the
head gate, attention run in that latent space, and a plain up-projection back (no norm). Q/K/V/O and the
gate now scale with `attn_latent_dim`, not the residual width.

**Sweep wiring** (`launch.py`): MoE rungs set `attn_latent_dim = hidden//2`. New `--residual-dim` overrides
only `hidden_dim`; `latent_dim`, `intermediate_dim`, shared/attn latent widths, `initializer_std`, the LR
recipe, and the token budget stay **pinned to the rung baseline**, so every point is data-matched with a
fixed attention/MoE compute core.

Data-matched: d512 family = 2,340 steps · 1.23B tokens; d768 family = 6,840 steps · 3.59B tokens; batch 128, seq 4096.

### FLOPs (total training, 3·fwd·tokens)

| family | residual | Δ vs base | active params | tokens | total FLOPs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **d512** (latent 256) | 384 | −128 | 18.2M | 1.23B | 2.38e17 |
| | 512 | base | 20.4M | 1.23B | 2.70e17 |
| | 640 | +128 | 22.7M | 1.23B | 3.02e17 |
| | 768 | +256 | 25.0M | 1.23B | 3.34e17 |
| | 1024 | +512 | 29.5M | 1.23B | 3.98e17 |
| | 1536 | +1024 | 38.5M | 1.23B | 5.27e17 |
| **d768** (latent 384) | 640 | −128 | 55.4M | 3.59B | 1.76e18 |
| | 768 | base | 59.8M | 3.59B | 1.90e18 |
| | 896 | +128 | 64.1M | 3.59B | 2.03e18 |
| | 1024 | +256 | 68.4M | 3.59B | 2.17e18 |
| | 1280 | +512 | 77.1M | 3.59B | 2.45e18 |
| | 1792 | +1024 | 94.4M | 3.59B | 3.00e18 |

The decoupling holds: a **4× wider residual** (384→1536) costs only **~2.2× FLOPs** at d512, and ~2.8× wider
(640→1792) costs ~1.7× at d768 — because attention + experts are pinned at the latent and only
embed/lm_head/projections/router/shared/norms grow with the residual.

W&B run ids: `fasttrack-reslat-{d512,d768}-r<width>` in `marin-community/marin_moe`. Paloma macro loss to follow.

*Note: the wandb-logged MFU will overcount (it prices attention at the residual width via `lm_flops_per_token`); the FLOPs above are the corrected analytic values used for reporting.*

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: As we scale up, the ratio of hidden_dim:vocab grows, so residual stream scaling gets relatively cheaper. At d2048 we can 2x the residual stream size for only a 18% increase in flops. We can get even stronger efficiency with smaller latents, such as 512 kv via MLA. No additional parameter cost or flop cost, just slightly higher activation memory. But the precedent for higher activation memory is already there with things like 4x manifold hyperconnections. And perhaps we can only save the latents on each layer for the bwk instead of the residual stream.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 ## Results: d512 & d768 residual-width sweep (all 12 finished)

Paloma macro loss, data-matched within each family, latent/attn/MoE compute held fixed. **Wider residual → monotonically lower loss** in both families.

| family | residual | Δ | Paloma loss | ΔL vs base | total FLOPs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **d512** (latent 256) | 384 | −128 | 3.2377 | +0.0572 | 2.38e17 |
| | 512 | base | 3.1804 | — | 2.70e17 |
| | 640 | +128 | 3.1685 | −0.0119 | 3.02e17 |
| | 768 | +256 | 3.1377 | −0.0428 | 3.34e17 |
| | 1024 | +512 | 3.1326 | −0.0478 | 3.98e17 |
| | 1536 | +1024 | **3.1170** | **−0.0634** | 5.27e17 |
| **d768** (latent 384) | 640 | −128 | 2.8948 | +0.0178 | 1.76e18 |
| | 768 | base | 2.8770 | — | 1.90e18 |
| | 896 | +128 | 2.8664 | −0.0105 | 2.03e18 |
| | 1024 | +256 | 2.8502 | −0.0268 | 2.17e18 |
| | 1280 | +512 | 2.8455 | −0.0314 | 2.45e18 |
| | 1792 | +1024 | **2.8293** | **−0.0477** | 3.00e18 |

### Takeaways

- **Monotone win with diminishing returns.** Widening the residual 3× at d512 (512→1536, only 1.95× FLOPs) buys −0.063 Paloma; 2.33× at d768 (768→1792, 1.58× FLOPs) buys −0.048. The residual stream is a cheap, reliable quality lever — exactly the trade the decoupling was built to expose.
- **The latent-attention base costs a little at equal width.** New base vs the original full-width MoE baseline: d512 3.1804 vs 3.156, d768 2.8770 vs 2.872 — compressing attention to the latent gives up ~0.02 at d512, ~neutral at d768. But residual widening more than buys it back: at d512 residual 768 (1.24× FLOPs) we reach 3.1377, already **below** the original full-width baseline.
- **MFU note:** the wandb-logged MFU rises with residual (6.5→16.4% at d512) only because it prices attention at the residual width; the analytic FLOPs above are the reference. Real throughput (tps) falls modestly as the residual grows (2.33M→1.56M at d512).

Plots: quality-vs-residual + loss-vs-compute are in the artifact and at `experiments/grug/fast_track/residual_quality.png`.

### In flight
The **d1280, 12-routed / no-shared** runs (residual 1280 / 1664 / 2560) are training (~10 hr) — first quality data for that leaner expert mix. The earlier d512/d768 12-routed/no-shared compute projections are analytic only so far.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## Goal

Honest replication of the paper's base-size experiment (Table 6) with a dense model: d8 (width 1024, ~210M params, vocab 50,304), 1B tokens of FineWeb with the GPT-2 tokenizer, batch 524,288, 2048-token sequences, under the paper's own Table 5 hyperparameters.

Three arms (branch `paper-replication`, variant `experiments/grug/paper_rep/`):

| Arm | Model | Recipe | Paper target (val loss) | Ours |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `vanilla` | plain transformer | Vanilla | 3.3279 | 3.2661 |
| `op1` | Operator-1 (K=1, 2/3/3 split, alpha 1) | Operator-1 | 3.3057 | 3.4738 |
| `op1-vanilla-recipe` | Operator-1 | Vanilla | 3.3135 | 3.2561 |

**Result:** the transfer probe replicates (Operator-1 under the vanilla recipe is −0.010 better than vanilla; paper: −0.014), but the central claim does not — the Operator-1 own recipe is +0.208 worse than vanilla instead of −0.022 better. Full analysis in the verdict comment below.

## Context

- Variant PR: #9293
- The MoE-vehicle ablation (#9280) showed the paper's recipe knobs (ELRM/HLRM/RM/OM/WTE/UIS/WD) do not exist in the MuonH template, which motivated this dense replication under the paper's own optimizer.
- Documented deviations (WD placement, Muon internals, the FineWeb 10BT slice, sequence packing) are listed in the variant README.

## Plan

- [x] Implement variant (`model.py`, `optimizer.py`, `recipes.py`, `data.py`, `train.py`, `launch.py`, tests)
- [x] Lint + tests green; PR open
- [x] Materialize FineWeb caches (one-time download + tokenize)
- [x] Run the three arms (~45 min each)
- [x] Compare against Table 6 and record the verdict (with W&B run links)

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 **Result: dense replication of the base-size experiment (d8, 1B tokens) — the architecture gain replicates, the Operator-1 own-recipe gain does not.**

All three arms completed (1907 steps, batch 524,288 tokens, seed 0, shared FineWeb caches, preemptible v4-16, ~45 min each). Final eval loss on the held-out FineWeb file (`eval/loss`, micro-average over 200×256×2048 ≈ 105M tokens):

| Arm | Ours | Paper (Table 6) | Δ ours−paper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vanilla | **3.2661** | 3.3279 | −0.062 |
| Operator-1, own recipe | **3.4738** | 3.3057 | +0.168 |
| Operator-1, vanilla recipe | **3.2561** | 3.3135 | −0.057 |

Eval-loss trajectories (steps 500 / 1000 / 1500 / 1907):

- vanilla: 3.7407 / 3.4931 / 3.3381 / 3.2661
- op1, own recipe: 4.1686 / 3.7217 / 3.5456 / 3.4738
- op1, vanilla recipe: 3.7563 / 3.4988 / 3.3317 / 3.2561

## What replicates

- **The transfer probe.** Operator-1 under the vanilla recipe beats plain vanilla by −0.0100 (paper: −0.0144). The K=1 boundary operator architecture is neutral-to-slightly-positive at this scale, matching the paper's direction and magnitude.
- **Absolute scale.** Our vanilla is 0.06 below the paper's number — expected given the documented deviations (FineWeb 10BT slice vs the full corpus, sequence packing without cross-doc attention masking, modded-nanogpt Muon internals, decoupled WD on the AdamW groups only, TPU vs the paper's H100s).

## What does not replicate

- **The paper's central claim for Operator-1**: own-recipe 3.3057 < vanilla 3.3279 (−0.022). We get the opposite sign at 10× the magnitude: own-recipe 3.4738 = **+0.208** vs our vanilla. The arm is behind from the first eval (4.17 vs 3.74 at step 500) and the gap never closes — a hyperparameter-configuration effect, not a training collapse.
- The recipe transcription was verified against paper Table 5 three separate times (most recently against the paper source): GLR 0.04, ELRM 0.905, HLRM 0.08, RM 0.5, OM 1, α<sub>emb</sub> 1, WD 0.05, WTE 0.113, UIS 0.354, WU 0, WDR 0.8, β 0.8/0.98, ε 1e-10. The LR schedule was verified step-by-step: constant GLR from step 0 (the paper specifies no warmup for Operator-1), linear warmdown over the last 80% to zero.

## Interpretation

Consistent with the Phase-0 MoE ablation (#9280): the boundary-operator architecture does not carry a robust gain in our stack, and the paper's Operator-1 advantage is not robust to the documented implementation deviations. The own-recipe inversion (paper −0.008 recipe benefit → our +0.218 penalty) points at recipe–implementation interactions — most plausibly WU=0 with full GLR 0.04 under our Muon, or the WTE/UIS/ELRM init-scale cluster — which the paper's reported numbers do not disambiguate. A knob-at-a-time ablation of the Operator-1 recipe under our implementation would isolate it (not done here).

## Runs

- Data: train cache `fineweb-10bt-gpt2@2026.09.19` (10.34B tokens / 14.87M docs), val `fineweb-val-gpt2@2026.09.19` (400k docs / 295.8M tokens)
- Vanilla: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/paper_rep_d8_vanilla
- Operator-1 own recipe: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/paper_rep_d8_op1
- Operator-1 vanilla recipe: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/paper_rep_d8_op1_vanilla_recipe

Variant: `experiments/grug/paper_rep/` (PR #9293). Infra note: the v4-8 pools were degraded at launch time, so arms ran on preemptible v4-16 (batch 256 divides evenly; global batch and data order unchanged, all arms identical hardware).

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Add and evaluate "standard" LLM architecture features on top of the fast_track MoE baseline, one
feature per branch (`fast_track_abl_<feature>`), each run at d512 and d768 and compared to the MoE
baseline (data-matched). Per agent.md, each feature gets an issue comment with its spec, branch link,
and results (Paloma/uncheatable bpb, throughput, params, FLOPs).

## Method

- Each feature is an **addition** to the current MoE baseline (not a hold-out ablation).
- Branch `fast_track_abl_<feature>` off the fast_track branch; toggle via a launcher flag/config.
- Run d512 + d768, data-matched to the MoE baseline budget (d512 = 2,385 steps, d768 = 6,930 steps,
  batch 128, seq 4096), on cw-us-east-02a. No checkpoints; eval on.
- Comment per feature: spec, branch, W&B runs, bpb (Paloma + uncheatable), throughput/MFU, params,
  FLOPs (±lm_head), 1–3 line takeaway.

## Features

### Well-specified (implementable now)
1. **MLA** — multi-head latent attention. KV latent size 512 with a learnable RMS norm; compress Q to
   512 with its own learnable RMS norm. (At d512 hidden this is ~no real compression — a structural test.)
2. **Cross-layer KV sharing** — the residual stream at the midpoint feeds KV for the final half of
   layers (every layer still keeps its own KV projection).
3. **Sandwich norm** — norm before *and* after each sublayer.
4. **Logit soft-capping** — tanh cap on attention and/or final logits.
5. **Learnable residual gain** — per-channel learnable scaling on residual adds (LayerScale-style).
6. **Parallel attention + FFN** — attention and MLP read the same block input (PaLM/GPT-J style).
7. **Tied embeddings** — share `token_embed` with `lm_head`.
8. **MTP** — multi-token prediction auxiliary head(s).

### Heavier / known but large
9. **Mamba-2** — replace ONLY the local sliding-window layers with Mamba-2; leave global attention.
10. **Gated DeltaNet 2** — same placement (local layers only).
11. **Kimi Linear** — same placement (local layers only).
12. **NSA** — native sparse attention.
13. **Over-encoding** — over-encoded input embeddings.

### Needs a spec/paper link (post-cutoff or under-specified for me)
14. **DeepSeek-V4 activation** on SwiGLU.
15. **DeepSeek-V4.1 attention design.**
16. **TST** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06546 (post my knowledge cutoff; will fetch/confirm spec).
17. **Block attention residuals.**
18. **Engram.**
19. **Manifold / hyper-connections.**

Skipping (from the top-30 list): #4 differential attention, #5 attention sinks.

## Links
* fast_track PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9287
* Ablation study (feature removals): #9288

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Resolved paper links / specs for the feature list (Kimi Linear = KDA confirmed):

**Attention / SSM**
- MLA — DeepSeek-V2, [arxiv 2405.04434](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434)
- Mamba-2 — [arxiv 2405.21060](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21060)
- Gated DeltaNet (base) — [arxiv 2412.06464](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06464); **Gated DeltaNet-2** (decouples erase/write; generalizes GDN + KDA) — [arxiv 2605.22791](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22791)
- Kimi Linear / **KDA** (Gated DeltaNet + fine-grained per-channel diagonal gating; hybrid w/ MLA) — [arxiv 2510.26692](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26692); ref impl: github.com/MoonshotAI (KDA)
- NSA — DeepSeek Native Sparse Attention, [arxiv 2502.11089](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11089)
- DeepSeek-V4 attention (CSA = compressed-KV + sparse DSA; HCA = heavy-compression dense; interleaved) — [arxiv 2606.19348](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348)
- DeepSeek-V4.1 attention (CSA2: per-layer Full/Reindex/Reuse KV sharing; two-tier 128-tok window + compressed-KV every ~6 layers; CED encoder-decoder) — no arxiv; [HF: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), [writeup](https://erogol.substack.com/p/deepseek-v41-flash-new-asymmetric)

**Residual / connections / norm**
- Block attention residuals — "Attention Residuals" (Kimi Team; learned depth-wise attention over layer outputs; Block-AttnRes groups ~8 blocks) — [arxiv 2603.15031](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), github.com/MoonshotAI/Attention-Residuals
- Manifold / hyper-connections — DeepSeek-V4's **mHC (Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections)** in [2606.19348](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348), built on **Hyper-Connections** [arxiv 2409.19606](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19606)
- Sandwich norm (Gemma-2), logit soft-cap (Gemma-2), learnable residual gain (LayerScale), parallel attn+FFN (PaLM/GPT-J) — standard, no paper fetch needed

**FFN / embeddings / memory / training**
- DeepSeek-V4 activation — clamped SwiGLU (clamp gate/up to a swiglu_limit; low-cost, no exp/div), from [2606.19348](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348)
- Over-encoding — "Over-Tokenized Transformer: Vocabulary is Worth Scaling" (large n-gram input vocab via tiled/decomposed embedding) — [arxiv 2501.16975](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16975)
- MTP — DeepSeek-V3, [arxiv 2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)
- Tied embeddings — standard
- Engram — DeepSeek "Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup" (hashed token n-gram O(1) lookup fused into residual via gating) — [arxiv 2601.07372](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372)
- **TST** — "Efficient Pre-Training with Token Superposition" [arxiv 2605.06546](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06546) — NB: this is a **training method** (superposition phase w/ multi-hot CE, then recovery), *not* an architecture change; it wouldn't be a per-feature model branch but a training-loop change.

🤖 ## Feature-addition results (d512 / d768 MoE, data-matched)

All 13 features run at d512 and d768 on cw-us-east-02a, data-matched to the MoE baseline
(d512 = 2,385 steps, d768 = 6,930 steps, batch 128, seq 4096). Reported in **Paloma macro loss**

**Effective speedup** vs baseline (fit L∞=1.2, α=0.0842): `Sc` = equal-tps compute speedup
`((L_base−1.2)/(L_feat−1.2))^(1/α)`; `Sw` = throughput-adjusted `Sc·(tps_feat/tps_base)`. **>1 = win.**

| feature | d512 L | ΔL | Sc | Sw | d768 L | ΔL | Sc | Sw |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **attn_residuals** | 3.1470 | **−0.0089** | 1.06 | 1.01 | 2.8508 | **−0.0216** | **1.17** | **1.19** |

| residual_gain | 3.1539 | −0.0020 | 1.01 | 0.93 | 2.8739 | +0.0016 | 0.99 | 1.01 |
| over_encoding | 3.1639 | +0.0080 | 0.95 | 0.87 | 2.8665 | −0.0058 | 1.04 | 1.04 |
| sandwich_norm | 3.1693 | +0.0134 | 0.92 | 0.84 | 2.8675 | −0.0048 | 1.04 | 1.05 |

| mla_d64r64 | 3.1781 | +0.0222 | 0.87 | 0.78 | 2.8690 | −0.0033 | 1.02 | 0.96 |
| mla_d128r64 | 3.1679 | +0.0121 | 0.93 | 0.16 | *running* | — | — | — |
| parallel_layers | 3.1982 | +0.0424 | 0.78 | 0.73 | 2.9009 | +0.0286 | 0.82 | 0.85 |

### Gate 1 (beats baseline at **both** scales)

- **Pass:** `attn_residuals`, `cross_layer_kv`, `tied_embed`, `mhc`. `attn_residuals` (Kimi) is the
  standout — the only feature with a >1% loss drop (−0.0216 at d768, Sc 1.17 / Sw 1.19) and it costs no throughput.
  `cross_layer_kv` and `tied_embed` are consistent smaller wins; `mhc` helps on loss but its d768 MFU dip (9.5%) pulls Sw below 1.
- **Marginal / neutral:** `logit_softcap` (~tie at d768), `residual_gain` (~tie).
- **Scale-dependent (hurts d512, helps d768):** `over_encoding`, `sandwich_norm`, `engram`, `mtp`, `mla_d64r64` — all fail gate 1 on the d512 regression.
- **Fail both:** `parallel_layers` (worst, +0.042 / +0.029).

### Notes

- **`mla_d128r64` MFU cliff:** the 192-dim head (nope 128 + rope 64) lands off the fa4_cute fast path →
  MFU 1.3% (tps 0.40M vs 2.34M baseline) at d512, so its `Sw`=0.16 reflects the kernel, not the architecture.
  `mla_d64r64` (128-dim head, on the fast path) runs at ~full speed. The d768 `mla_d128r64` run is still going
  (same slow kernel) and will be folded in when it finishes.
- `mtp` and `mla_*` carry a real throughput tax (extra dense MTP block / smaller attention heads); the rest are throughput-neutral.

Recommendation: promote **attn_residuals** and **cross_layer_kv** to the full ladder (gate 2, d1024/d1280);
**tied_embed** is a cheap consistent win worth carrying alongside.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
The Snowball v83 64-GPU Megatron run lost its step-2 checkpoint after at least two policy ranks received S3 errors. Other ranks completed their uploads and waited in the final checkpoint barrier. Thirty minutes later, rank 9 timed out on a one-element `ALLREDUCE`; the NCCL watchdog aborted the policy workers. The trainer had already recorded `checkpoint_save_failures=1` and continued generating step 3, but no complete checkpoint or latest-step pointer was published.

Reproduce:
1. Launch the [v83 run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fbenfeuer%2Fsnowball-rlvr1-bs512-gs16-sft-passn-step159000-v83-32k-bounded-s3-20260916-coord-v83%2Fsnowball-rlvr1-bs512-gs16-sft-passn-step159000-v83-32k-bounded-s3-20260916) at runtime `598d5f64b` with S3 checkpoints every two optimizer steps.
2. Have one policy-rank upload fail while other ranks finish. In this run, `CreateMultipartUpload` returned `SlowDown: Please reduce your request rate`, and another rank's s3fs upload called `CreateBucket` and received `InvalidRegion: Region does not match`.
3. Observe successful ranks waiting at [megatron_strategy.py:243](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/598d5f64b6f704b62f8f4a347b5da03f095fc624/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/distributed/megatron/megatron_strategy.py#L243) while failed ranks skip that barrier. Rank 9 reported `WorkNCCL(SeqNum=2985, OpType=ALLREDUCE, NumelIn=1, Timeout(ms)=1800000)` at 01:43:44 UTC and the workers aborted at 01:48:44 UTC.

Expected: An upload error reaches every checkpoint participant within a bounded time. The trainer either retries a consistent save or stops without leaving live ranks in a collective or continuing against a broken policy mesh. No latest-step pointer should be published for a partial save.

The first error occurred at 01:09:30 UTC on September 17. Rank logs under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/skyrl/users/benfeuer/snowball-rlvr1-bs512-gs16-sft-passn-step159000-v83-32k-bounded-s3-20260916/ray_session_logs/` preserve the S3 errors, barrier stack, and watchdog timeout; process outcomes are under the sibling `rendezvous/debug_artifacts/` prefix. [MarinSkyRL #665](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/665) replaces staged uploads with direct S3 writes and finite request deadlines; v83 predates it. The cross-rank failure path has not been validated with an injected S3 error.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
Tracking issue for testing the optimizations identified in #8053 against the 1-rack FSDP hero. Analysis and profile links are in #8053; this issue records the measurement protocol and the measured result of each arm.

Measurement protocol

Each arm is a 20-step single-rack run (64x GB200, batch 1024 x seq 4096) with `--no-save-checkpoints --watch-interval 0`. Steps 0-1 are compile and the PGLE recompile (146 s and 108 s in the reference run); steps 2-4 absorb the one-time first-batch data-loader stall. The score is the median `throughput/duration` over steps 5-19.

Median rather than mean, because the steady-state distribution is right-skewed. The reference run (`gprof-xprof-1rack-20260807`) over steps 5-19 gives median 18.086 s, MAD 0.077 s, min 17.936 s, max 18.699 s, stdev 0.210 s (1.16%). The median's standard error at n=15 is about 0.068 s, so a 2-sigma within-run effect is 0.14 s, roughly 0.15 MFU points.

Within-run noise is not the binding constraint; run-to-run variation from node allocation and recompilation is. Every wave therefore launches a `control` arm with the unmodified configuration in the same wall-clock window, on one of the four racks. An arm counts as a win only when it beats the control by more than the control-to-control spread. MFU is reported for readability but carries no information beyond step time, since the FLOP denominator is fixed by the shape.

Four racks at production priority run one control plus three experiment arms per wave, about 15 minutes per wave.

Arms to test, in expected-uplift order

| Wave | Arm | Change | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `simple` | `NCCL_PROTO=Simple` | +1.5 to +3 |
| 1 | `ll128` | `NCCL_PROTO=LL128` | +1.5 to +3 |
| 1 | `nvls` | `NCCL_ALGO=NVLS,Ring`, `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=1` | +1.5 to +3 |
| 2 | `combine` | Raise the XLA all-gather and reduce-scatter combiner thresholds | +0.3 to +1 |
| 2 | `pipelined` | `--xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_all_gather`, `..._reduce_scatter` | +0.3 to +0.8 |
| 2 | `nopgle` | `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=0`, isolated from the nsys overhead that confounded the first estimate | 0 |
| 3 | `shard-small` | FSDP-shard router, `attn_gate`, and both `GatedNorm` factor pairs | +0.5 to +0.8 |
| 3 | `interleave` | Interleave w13 before the expert-weight all-gather instead of after | +0.6 to +1.0 |
| 3 | `chunks` | `expert_chunks` sweep and an unequal first chunk | +0.3 to +0.7 |
| 4 | `offload-act` | `remat_mode="save_moe"` with `save_and_offload_only_these_names` to Grace | +2 to +4 |
| 4 | `wgrad` | MoE weight-grad on the CUTLASS grouped GEMM instead of XLA `ragged_dot` | +1 to +1.5 |
| 5 | `combined` | Every arm that won, stacked | — |

Peak HBM logging lands before wave 3 so every later arm reports `peak_bytes_in_use`; today nothing in the training path records it, which is why the 160 GB to 154 GB regression could not be attributed from the profile.

Results are posted per wave as comments, and consolidated into this issue body at the end.

Part of #8053

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wave 1 results: NCCL protocol and algorithm.

The protocol validates. The wave-1 control landed at 18.101 s against the reference run's 18.086 s, a 0.08% drift across a different node allocation and a separate compilation, so between-run variation is far below within-run noise. Median standard error at n=15 is about 0.027 s, putting the 2-sigma bar at 0.053 s, or 0.29%.

| arm | median (steps 5-19) | MAD | min | MFU | vs control |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `nvls` (`NCCL_ALGO=NVLS,Ring`, `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=1`) | 17.978 s | 0.055 s | 17.830 s | 19.46% | +0.68% |
| `simple` (`NCCL_PROTO=Simple`) | 18.068 s | 0.047 s | 17.982 s | 19.37% | +0.19% |
| `control` | 18.101 s | 0.056 s | 17.984 s | 19.33% | — |
| `ll128` (`NCCL_PROTO=LL128`) | 18.590 s | 0.066 s | 18.425 s | 18.82% | -2.70% |

NVLS is a real but small win: 0.123 s, 4.6 sigma, worth 0.13 MFU points. `Simple` is 1.2 sigma and indistinguishable from the control. `LL128` is a clear regression.

This falsifies the expected +1.5 to +3 for this arm. The profile showed the MoE expert-weight all-gather achieving 429 GB/s and the expert-grad reduce-scatter 445 GB/s, both about 48% of NVLink-5's 900 GB/s per-GPU unidirectional, and #8053 flagged that xprof measures NCCL kernel duration including the wait for the slowest peer. Switching protocol changes how bytes move and barely moves the step time, so the missing half of the link is peer wait, not protocol overhead. That reweights the remaining work: the per-layer barriers and the routing imbalance feeding them matter more than collective bandwidth, and the `shardsmall` arm that removes a 64-way all-reduce from every scan iteration is now the more interesting of the cheap arms.

Carrying `NVLS` into the final combined arm.

Separately, PGLE has never been working in this configuration. The runs log `PGLE collected an empty trace, may be due to contention with another tool that subscribes to CUPTI`, and the reference profiling run logged it 32 times, twice per process across all 16 processes, with no external profiler attached. The earlier estimate in #8053 that PGLE contributes at most 0.22 MFU points was therefore comparing broken PGLE against no PGLE. Nothing in the training path starts a trace during these runs, so the subscriber is node-level; DCGM-exporter's profiling counters are the usual cause on a managed Kubernetes cluster. The consequence for the rest of this sweep is that XLA's latency-hiding scheduler has been ordering collectives from static cost estimates, which raises rather than lowers the value of the overlap work in #8053.

Wave 2 is running: `shardsmall` (FSDP-shard router, `attn_gate`, both `GatedNorm` factor pairs), `interleave` (interleave w13 on the local shard before the all-gather), and `savemoe` (`remat_mode="save_moe"`, which probes the HBM ceiling and may OOM). Each is now a launcher flag defaulting to today's behavior, because Iris ships the local worktree to the job and all four racks in a wave share one code state. Peak HBM is logged from this wave on.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wave 2 results: the two cheap code changes both win, and the HBM question is answered.

| arm | median (steps 5-19) | MAD | MFU | peak HBM | vs control |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `shardsmall` (FSDP-shard router, `attn_gate`, both `GatedNorm` factor pairs) | 17.377 s | 0.066 s | 20.13% | 148.9 GiB | +2.73% |
| `interleave` (interleave w13 on the local shard before the all-gather) | 17.590 s | 0.030 s | 19.89% | 139.8 GiB | +1.54% |
| `control` | 17.865 s | 0.069 s | 19.59% | 140.9 GiB | — |
| `savemoe` (`remat_mode="save_moe"`) | OOM | | | | |

`shardsmall` is +0.54 MFU points, at the top of the +0.5 to +0.8 predicted in #8053. `interleave` is +0.30 points, below the +0.6 to +1.0 predicted, for a two-line change whose output is bitwise identical.

Both are consistent with the corrected step model. Neither hides work; both delete it.

Caveat on comparing across waves. The wave-2 control ran at 17.865 s against wave 1's 18.101 s, a 1.3% gap, well outside the 0.29% 2-sigma bar. Wave 1 and wave 2 ran from different code states, since wave 2 carried the new config fields and the unconditional reshards at the small-parameter use sites, and they drew different node allocations 20 minutes apart. Within-wave deltas remain valid, which is the reason for a control on every wave, but per-arm deltas from different waves must not be summed. The final combined arm is measured end-to-end against its own control.

The HBM question from #8053 candidate 4 is settled. XLA logs `hlo_rematerialization.cc:3282: Can't reduce memory use below <N>GiB` on every arm: 160.30 GiB on the control and on `interleave`, and 159.32 GiB on `shardsmall`. That warning is the "160 GB" number from the original brief. The rematerialization pass recomputes ops until peak memory fits the limit and reports the floor it could not get under, which is the mechanism behind "160 GB to 154 GB cost 1.5 MFU": a smaller limit forces more recompute, and that recompute is the 5.09 s/step already measured across 244 flagged HLO ops. Peak memory sits pinned against that floor, so freed HBM converts directly into recompute avoided. Peak HBM is now logged per step as `memory/peak_gib`.

`save_moe` is not viable at this shape and the failure is quantitative: `cuMemAllocAsync failed to allocate 415152102304 bytes`, 386.7 GiB, against a 138.22 GiB device limit. On the FSDP `sonic_cute` path only two of the four `MOE_REMAT_SAVE_NAMES` tags are ever applied, `grug_moe_dispatch_input` and `grug_moe_dispatch_output`, each about 155 GB across the 48 layers, which matches that allocation request.

That also rules out offloading all four tags, since a 4-GPU node gives each rank roughly 212 GiB of Grace LPDDR and the optimizer already holds a pinned-host arena. A new `offload_moe` remat mode therefore offloads only `grug_moe_dispatch_output` via `save_and_offload_only_these_names(offload_dst="pinned_host")`. That is the tag worth its C2C traffic: keeping it stops the backward from re-running the expert GEMMs and the expert-weight all-gather that feeds them, together 2.76 s/step, for about 310 GB/step of round-trip C2C, or 17 GB/s against a link of roughly 225 GB/s per direction.

Wave 3 is running: `combo` (both wave-2 winners together), `cebig` (`--ce-b-block-size 8192`, since cross-entropy launches 43,661 kernels per step at 16% of peak because `b_block_size` sits at its 1024 default), and `chunks8`. `offload_moe` goes in wave 4.

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 Re-analysed the reference capture from 4ab8ea5 in [HolisticTraceAnalysis](https://github.com/facebookresearch/HolisticTraceAnalysis), working from the XPlane timeline per stream. Five additions to the battery, two of which are already in the issue body and haven't had a slot yet.

Starting point: the step-model correction above and this analysis produce **the same numbers with different bookkeeping**. Worth reconciling, because the difference is what decides whether `pipelined` is worth a wave.

## The 16.28 s "main compute stream busy" includes 2.15 s of NCCL

Interval union per stream, rank 0, `ProfilerStep#1`:

| | s/step |
|---|---|
| main compute stream busy (the 16.28 s above) | 16.72 |
| — of which real compute kernels | 14.53 |
| — **of which NCCL kernels on the compute stream** | **2.15** |
| side-stream collective running alone (the 1.02 s above) | 0.91 |
| device fully idle | 0.25–0.37 |

That 2.15 s is `ncclDevKernel_AllGather_RING_LL` sitting in the compute queue, and it overlaps essentially nothing:

```
rank 0: compute-stream NCCL = 2153.1 ms, overlapped by compute = 0.2 ms (0.01%)
rank 1: compute-stream NCCL = 1982.4 ms, overlapped by compute = 0.2 ms (0.01%)
rank 2: compute-stream NCCL = 2128.0 ms, overlapped by compute = 0.2 ms (0.01%)
rank 3: compute-stream NCCL = 1943.3 ms, overlapped by compute = 0.2 ms (0.01%)
```

So total exposed collective time reads as 2.15 (main) + 0.91 (side) = **3.07 s**. The 1.02 s figure is side-stream exposure only — collectives on the main stream land inside "busy". Amusingly the 3.17 s in the original body was derived by a method that really is invalid (summing `hlo_stats` self-times double-counts across streams) but lands within 3% of the interval-union answer.

The SM-occupancy point is right and worth a number: NCCL kernels launch **32 blocks of the 152 SMs (21%)**. A hidden collective costs a fifth of the GPU; an exposed one leaves 120 SMs idle. That makes compute-stream collective time the most reclaimable block in the step rather than the least.

Wave 2 is the check on this. `all-reduce.213` runs on the compute stream, so under the corrected model it sits inside the 16.28 s and isn't reclaimable — but `shardsmall` removed it and won +2.73%, five times wave 1's best and 4.5× its own prediction. Measured here beforehand: `all-reduce.213` is 547 ms/step and **98% arrival-wait** — mean enter spread across the four ranks 8,327 µs, mean exit spread **2.5 µs**, corr(wait, duration) 0.77. 8.2 MiB across 64 GPUs is 19 µs of transfer at link speed; it takes 10,574 µs. Wave 2 recovered 488 ms of that.

If that holds up, the "no bubble to reclaim" line probably wants revisiting, and candidates 1 and 2 come back onto the table.

## Arm 1 — `pipelined` (in the issue body, displaced from wave 2)

The forward MoE expert-weight gathers are synchronous. The identical backward ones are asynchronous.

| hlo_op | placement | n | ms | GiB out | span | phase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `all_gather.82.1` | **SYNC** | 48 | 220.0 | 2.25 | 0.09→4.75 s | fwd |
| `all_gather.84.1` | **SYNC** | 48 | 215.9 | 2.25 | 0.09→4.75 s | fwd |
| `all_gather.80.1` | **SYNC** | 48 | 213.4 | 2.25 | 0.09→4.74 s | fwd |
| `all_gather.87.1` | **SYNC** | 48 | 120.9 | 1.12 | 0.08→4.74 s | fwd |
| `all_gather.83.1` | **SYNC** | 48 | 120.0 | 1.12 | 0.08→4.74 s | fwd |
| `all_gather.81.1` | **SYNC** | 48 | 115.8 | 1.12 | 0.08→4.73 s | fwd |
| | | | **1,006** | | | **0.01% overlapped** |
| `all_gather.100.1` | async | 47 | 285.5 | 2.25 | 6.14→17.41 s | bwd, ~80% hidden |
| `all_gather.96.1` | async | 47 | 229.1 | 2.25 | 6.13→17.40 s | bwd, ~80% hidden |

Six of eight forward gathers sync, eight of eight backward async. Compute density follows: **fwd 66.3%, bwd 87.3%**.

The mechanism is the one candidate 2 describes — with a 1-layer scan body the gathered weights are consumed in the same iteration, so the scheduler has no independent work to place between `-start` and `-done` and falls back to synchronous. `--xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_all_gather` / `..._reduce_scatter` aim at exactly this.

## Arm 2 — PGLE working, rather than `nopgle`

The empty-trace finding from wave 1 is very likely the cause of arm 1's symptom: with no profile, the latency-hiding scheduler ordered collectives from static cost estimates and left 717 of them per step on the compute stream.

4ab8ea5 is what makes this arm constructible — switching `os.environ.update` to `setdefault` means a launcher-forwarded `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE` now survives, where before the hero defaults would have clobbered it. What it doesn't do is make PGLE functional; that change targets the nsys direction (reliably turning PGLE *off*). And the warning count points node-level rather than at anything in-process: two per process across all 16 processes, while `--profile-start-step` only captures on process 0, so processes 1–15 would be clean if the XPlane capture were the competing subscriber.

Suggested gate for whoever runs it: grep the job log for `PGLE collected an empty trace` and don't score the arm if it's present, otherwise it re-measures broken PGLE and books a null.

## Arm 3 — `all-reduce.214`: 1,540 bytes taking 3.1 ms, 48×/step

Not currently tracked. From the HLO it's a flat `f32[385]` (not a tuple), one per layer: **1,540 bytes**, 48×/step, **189 ms/step**, compute stream, 100% exposed. The kernel is `ncclDevKernel_AllReduce_Sum_f32_RING_LL` with a **grid of 1 block** — 151 of 152 SMs idle for 3.1 ms. CV 0.579, p95/p05 = 11.07. Pure barrier, no meaningful transfer.

`shardsmall` doesn't remove it — that removed the 4,288,512-element bf16 one.

Best guess at the source is the router telemetry: `_routing_stats` (`model.py:623`) returns `routing_counts[128]` plus scalar `routing_entropy` / `load_balancing_loss` / `router_z_loss` per layer, stacked at `model.py:1004-1013`. That's 131 f32 per layer, not 385, so XLA's all-reduce combiner is presumably merging a few of these — someone closer to the router path can confirm what the other 254 are. `report_capacity_overflow` is `False` by default and only referenced from `moe_hero_ep`, so `grug_moe.py:311` is not it.

Worth checking whether these stats are live at all under `--watch-interval 0`. If they're only consumed by logging, gating them off is 48 barriers → 0 for ~189 ms/step.

## Arm 4 — `reduce-scatter.24` is also synchronous

415 MB in / 6.5 MB out, 47×/step, 164 ms, compute stream, 100% exposed, CV 0.409 (part barrier, part transfer). Worth re-checking whether `shardsmall` moved it.

A diagnostic rather than an arm: it is **systematically rank-3-late in 40 of 47 instances**, where `all-reduce.213` is random (9/16/9/13 last-to-arrive). Systematic lateness on one rank is a load-imbalance signal rather than jitter.

## Arm 5 — `combine`, also in the body and not yet run

768 all-gathers per step at 36 MiB achieving **43 GB/s, 5% of link**, ~915 ms/step. Combiner thresholds target this directly. Possibly partly obsoleted by `shardsmall`, so worth a re-capture before spending a slot.

## Why wave 1 came out flat — and a correction to my own number

An earlier pass of this analysis put the large gathers at 515 GB/s. That was wrong — it subtracted arrival wait before dividing. Per-instance the figure is **390–500 GB/s, 43–56% of link**, so the body's 429 GB/s / 48% was accurate.

But the reading that "the missing half of the link is peer wait" doesn't seem to hold for the large gathers. Discriminating on duration stability:

| op | size | CV | p95/p05 | cross-rank corr |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `all_gather.100.1` | 2,304 MiB | **0.031** | 1.10 | +0.987 |
| `all_gather.86.1` | 2,304 MiB | **0.046** | 1.17 | +0.993 |
| `all-reduce.213` | 8.2 MiB | 0.429 | 5.95 | +0.174 |
| `all-reduce.214` | 1.5 KiB | 0.579 | 11.07 | — |

Step-to-step means for `all_gather.86.1` are 5772 / 5800 / 5838 µs, reproducible to 1%. A collective inheriting a randomly-late peer's jitter can't have CV 0.031, so those gathers look wire-bound.

The wave-1 conclusion still stands, just for a different reason: the collective workload is bimodal — roughly 380 large wire-bound gathers (CV 0.03) and 768 small latency-bound ones (36 MiB, CV 0.29) per step. A global `NCCL_PROTO` has to serve both, so `Simple` helps the large and hurts the small (net +0.19%) and `LL128` hurts the small badly (−2.70%). The −2.70% is itself evidence that protocol moves step time — under pure peer-wait it couldn't move in either direction. The untested variant is per-collective selection (`NCCL_ALGO="allgather:nvls;..."`) rather than a global switch.

## One suggestion for the protocol

Median step time at a 0.29% 2-sigma bar says whether an arm worked but not why, and wave-to-wave control drift (1.3% between waves 1 and 2) already exceeds it. A 3-step XPlane capture gives a direct and much more sensitive readout:

> **collective ms on the compute stream vs the side stream** — today 2,051 vs 4,504

For `pipelined`, PGLE and `combine` that one number says whether the mechanism engaged, independently of run-to-run noise. Same idea as the `bf16[4288512]` disappearance check already proposed for `shardsmall`, generalised.

For wave 4, `offload_moe`'s C2C DMA can fail the same way these collectives do — worth confirming the copies land on a dedicated stream before reading the arm.

## Caveats

Four of 64 ranks, all co-resident on one host, so the cross-rank skew figures are lower bounds: uniform lateness among the other 60 would show up as all four ranks waiting in lockstep. The duration-stability test is what rules that out for the large gathers; it can't rule it out for the small ones.

This is the reference capture — PGLE broken, pre-`shardsmall`, pre-`interleave` — so the sync/async split may well have moved. A fresh 3-step capture on the wave-3 `combo` arm would re-baseline all of the above cheaply.

Two things checked that turned out to be nothing, noted so they don't get re-litigated: there's no wave-quantization or grid-underfill opportunity. The XPlane device plane reports `core_count = 152`, which makes QuACK's fixed `(2,1,76)` = 152-CTA grid an exact one-wave fit, and only 31 ms/step (0.2% of compute) runs on kernels of ≤8 blocks. Candidate 14's 50%-of-peak stays unexplained.

Also worth recording since candidate 4 called for it: the device plane carries `gpu_device_name = NVIDIA GB200`, `core_count = 152`, `clock_rate = 2062 MHz`, `memory_bandwidth = 7.93 TB/s`, `memory_size = 197.9 GB`. Capacity and bandwidth are in every capture even though usage wasn't, which puts the 154 GB working set at about 78% of the device.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wave 3 results. Stacking the two wave-2 winners beats the sum of their parts; cross-entropy tiling is a dead end; and activation offloading is out of reach at this shape for a second, different reason.

| arm | median (steps 5-19) | MAD | MFU | peak HBM | vs control |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `combo` (`--small-param-sharding fsdp --interleave-before-gather`) | 16.767 s | 0.015 s | 20.87% | 137.2 GiB | +6.42% |
| `control` | 17.917 s | 0.099 s | 19.53% | 140.9 GiB | — |
| `cebig` (`--ce-b-block-size 8192`) | 17.921 s | 0.087 s | 19.52% | 150.0 GiB | −0.02% |
| `offloadmoe` (`--remat-mode offload_moe`) | host OOM | | | | |

`combo` is +1.34 MFU points, against +0.54 and +0.30 for the same two changes measured separately in wave 2. The parts predict +4.3%; together they deliver +6.4%.

The extra 2 points are not a measurement artifact. `combo`'s MAD is 0.015 s, the tightest of any arm so far and 6x tighter than its own control, and its peak HBM drops to 137.2 GiB against the control's 140.9 GiB. That is the mechanism: XLA's rematerialization pass recomputes until peak memory fits the limit and reports the floor it could not get under, so the two changes pay twice. They delete work directly, and the memory they free buys back recompute that the control is forced to do. This is the same lever behind the "160 GB to 154 GB cost 1.5 MFU" observation in #8053, running in the profitable direction.

`cebig` does nothing, at a cost. Raising the cross-entropy token block from 1024 to 8192 moved the median by −0.02%, inside noise, while peak HBM rose 9.1 GiB. The 43,661 kernel launches per step are real but they are not what the fused cross-entropy is limited by, and on the evidence above, 9 GiB of extra peak is actively harmful. Not pursuing this.

`offload_moe` fails on host memory, not device memory, which is a different wall than `save_moe` hit. The offloaded dispatch output needs a 144.00 GiB pinned-host arena and `xla_gpu_host_bfc` cannot get it: a rank has roughly 212 GiB of Grace LPDDR and the offloaded optimizer state already holds a large share. So at the hero shape, keeping the MoE dispatch tensors costs 386.7 GiB of HBM against a 138.22 GiB limit, and parking just the expert output costs 144 GiB of host RAM that is already spoken for.

Offloading a subset of layers would fit, but it is not expressible today. All 48 layers run under one `jax.scan` with a single remat policy, so "offload every other layer" requires breaking the scan, which is candidate 2 in #8053 and a much larger change. Recording this as the blocker rather than working around it.

Wave 4 is running: `combined` (both winners plus the wave-1 `NCCL_ALGO=NVLS,Ring` setting) measured end to end against its own same-window control, plus `chunks8` and `chunks2` for the MoE chunking question.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Interim status: where the sweep stands after five waves, and the next set of arms.

## Result so far

A configuration change with no effect on numerics takes the hero from **19.48% to 21.14% MFU**, **+1.66 points**, a 7.85% throughput gain, measured end to end against a control launched in the same window:

```
--small-param-sharding fsdp --interleave-before-gather
NCCL_ALGO=NVLS,Ring  NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=1
```

| Change | Delta | Verdict |
|---|---:|---|
| **Combined** | **+7.85%**, +1.66 pts | adopt |
| FSDP-shard router / `attn_gate` / `GatedNorm` factors | +2.73%, +0.54 pts | adopt |
| Interleave gate/up before the all-gather | +1.54%, +0.30 pts | adopt |
| `NCCL_ALGO=NVLS,Ring` | +0.68% | adopt |
| `NCCL_PROTO=Simple` | +0.19% | noise, drop |
| `NCCL_PROTO=LL128` | −2.70% | reject |
| CE token block 1024 → 8192 | −0.02%, +9.1 GiB | reject |
| `expert_chunks` 4 → 8 | −2.91%, +3.3 GiB | reject |
| `remat_mode="save_moe"` | device OOM at 386.7 GiB | infeasible |
| `remat_mode="offload_moe"` | host OOM at 144.0 GiB | infeasible |

The two code changes compound rather than add: +0.54 and +0.30 points separately, +1.34 together. Both free HBM, and XLA's rematerialization pass recomputes until peak fits under the allocator limit, so freed memory converts directly into recompute avoided.

Wave 5 is in flight (rerun of `chunks2`, plus `chunks1`, plus a replication of `combined` in a fresh window). Full write-up: https://loom.oa.dev/s/kwwm1q60/artifacts/report-sweep

## The next set of arms

**We are running the hero on 75% of the HBM on the part.** Nothing in the repo sets `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION`, so it sits at JAX's 0.75 default:

| | GiB |
|---|---|
| physical HBM per GPU | ~184.3 |
| allocator `bytes_limit` | **138.22** |
| `combined` peak | 137.21 |
| XLA's reported rematerialization floor | **160.30** |

XLA states it cannot get peak below 160.30 GiB without recomputing, against a limit 22 GiB lower. That gap is where the measured 5.09 s/step of backward recompute, 28% of the step, comes from. This is the same lever behind "160 GB down to 154 GB cost 1.5 MFU", except the memory was never missing: it was never offered.

Wave 6, all arms carrying the adopted configuration, with `base` as the control:

| arm | change | rationale |
|---|---|---|
| `base` | adopted config | this wave's control |
| `memfrac88` | `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.88` | 162.2 GiB, just above the 160.30 GiB floor |
| `memfrac93` | `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.93` | 171.4 GiB; may OOM, since NCCL and cuBLAS workspaces sit outside the pool |
| `ceautotune` | `LEVANTER_PALLAS_CE_AUTOTUNE_ON_MISS=1` | CE block sizes come from a shape bucket, not from this shape |

`memory/limit_gib` is logged per step, so an arm that silently ignores the knob under the `cuda_async` allocator shows up in the result rather than passing as a null effect.

## Correction

Two claims in the earlier analysis (#8053) do not survive.

The step model was wrong. Summing xprof `hlo_stats` self-times and calling the remainder a bubble double-counts across concurrent streams. From the XPlane timeline union, per 18.0 s step: the compute stream is busy 16.28 s (90.3%), a collective runs alone for 1.02 s (5.6%), and the device is fully idle for 0.49 s (2.7%). There is no 3.17 s bubble and no 23.6% overlap ceiling. This is why every measured win deletes compute-stream work rather than hiding it, and why NCCL tuning, ranked 2nd at +1.5 to +3 points, returned +0.68%.

There is also no GPU Pallas cross-entropy kernel. The implementations are `xla`, `batched_xla`, `reference`, and `pallas_tpu`; the Pallas one is TPU-only, so the earlier claim that this configuration was failing to use a shipped fused kernel was wrong. `batched_xla` remains untested here: it caps its `h*v` tile near 99 KB and cannot take `v_block_size=4096`, which is a tradeoff rather than a disqualification.

## Ranked after that

1. **Allocator fraction** (wave 6). Attacks 28% of the step, pure environment change.
2. **Break the 1-layer `jax.scan`.** No longer an overlap argument. All 48 layers share one remat policy, which is why per-layer offloading is inexpressible and why both memory strategies failed whole-model.
3. **FA4 is not running an SM100 kernel on GB200**: 1.27 s/step at 211 TFLOP/s, 8% of peak.
4. **CUDA graphs (#5675).** Cross-entropy alone dispatches 43,661 kernels per step averaging 17.5 µs, fully exposed because the hero sets `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=` empty.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wave 6: the HBM allocator fraction does nothing, and a mechanism I asserted earlier in this issue is wrong.

| arm | `bytes_limit` | peak HBM | median | MFU | vs `combined` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| w5 `combined` | 138.22 GiB | 137.21 GiB | 16.426 s | 21.30% | — |
| `memfrac88` | **162.18 GiB** | 137.21 GiB | 16.565 s | 21.12% | ~0 |
| `memfrac93` | **171.40 GiB** | 137.21 GiB | 16.637 s | 21.03% | −0.43% |

The knob took effect. `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` moved the allocator limit by 33 GiB, exactly the computed values, under the `cuda_async` allocator. Peak never moved off 137.21 GiB and step time did not improve. Logging `memory/limit_gib` per step is what separates this from an ambiguous null: the memory was offered and nothing took it.

## Why, and the correction

The hero's recompute comes from the explicit `remat_mode="recompute_all"` `jax.checkpoint` policy, which is fixed at trace time. XLA's `HloRematerialization` pass is a separate mechanism that only engages when peak exceeds the allocator limit. The control sits at 140.90 GiB against a 138.22 GiB limit, so it is engaged, which is the `Can't reduce memory use below 160.30GiB` message. The adopted configuration sits at 137.21 GiB, already under the limit, so that pass is not binding and raising the ceiling changes nothing.

This retracts the explanation in the interim comment above, which said the two adopted code changes compound because "both free HBM, and XLA's rematerialization pass recomputes until peak fits under the allocator limit, so freed memory converts directly into recompute avoided." That is not why. A second piece of evidence pointed the same way and was not weighted at the time: `shardsmall` alone raised peak HBM to 148.9 GiB, above the control's 140.9 GiB, and was still the single largest win.

The superadditivity itself is measured and reproducible: +0.54 and +0.30 MFU points separately, +1.34 together. Its mechanism is now unexplained. Part of the apparent magnitude may be control drift, since the wave controls moved 17.865 → 17.917 → 17.966 → 18.067 s while `combined` moved 16.767 → 16.555 → 16.426 s, both drifting in the direction that flatters the delta. The end-to-end `combined` measurement against a same-window control is unaffected by this and stands at +7.85% and +9.08% in two independent windows.

## What this means for spending the 46 GiB

The memory is genuinely unused and there is currently no consumer for it. Spending it is blocked where the earlier memory work was blocked:

- `save_moe` needs 386.7 GiB, still far past the raised 171.40 GiB limit.
- Saving or offloading a subset of layers would fit in the extra 33 GiB, but all 48 layers share one `jax.scan` with a single remat policy, so per-layer policy is not expressible.

Breaking the 1-layer scan is now the blocker for three separate things: activation offloading, partial activation saving, and any use of the freed HBM. It was ranked 13th of 15 in #8053 on overlap grounds, which the corrected step model already invalidated. It is now the highest-value structural item.

## Arms that did not report

`base` and `ceautotune` both died from node faults, 9 and 6 failures with sibling co-schedule bounces and no Python traceback. This is the third infrastructure fault in three waves, after `chunks2` in wave 4. The wave-6 conclusion does not depend on `base`, since both surviving arms land inside the established `combined` range of 16.43 to 16.56 s, but the cross-entropy autotuner is still unmeasured and will be rerun.

Wave 7 is running: CUDA graphs at NVIDIA's recommended `FUSION,CUSTOM_CALL`, collective combine thresholds at 512MB, and the two scheduler flags the EP hero already runs in production. Waves 8 and 9 cover the rest of the NVIDIA Blackwell guidance, none of which this repo sets today; the `O1` optimization level is the item to watch, because it enables the analytical SOL latency estimator, which is the direct substitute for the PGLE that has never collected a non-empty trace on this cluster.
