comments.body:
🤖 Queuing the native-SM100 FA4 subseries from `7810d9e2fd`.

The source audit found that the hero's `gpu_fa4_cute` backend is the custom segmented Ampere/SM120 fork (64x64, 128 threads on compute capability 10.x), while the existing `gpu_fa4_thd` backend dispatches the pinned upstream SM100 forward/backward classes (128x128 and SM100 two-CTA backward). This is not a missing build flag: the hero was dropping THD segment metadata and encoding its scanned local/global choice only as custom-kernel bounds.

Run matrix, launched in one window on `cw-us-east-08a`:

- `fa4sm100-w1-cute-a`: current segmented backend, unprofiled
- `fa4sm100-w1-cute-profile`: current segmented backend, XPlane steps 10-12
- `fa4sm100-w1-thd-a`: native SM100 THD backend, unprofiled
- `fa4sm100-w1-thd-profile`: native SM100 THD backend, XPlane steps 10-12

Each arm is a 20-step, 4-node/16-GPU GB200 FSDP run of a 15.44B-total, 869.8M-active model at sequence length 4096 and batch 512. Checkpoints and optimizer offload are disabled; outputs expire after 30 days. The throughput score is median step duration over steps 5-19, excluding profile capture steps for profiled arms. DRI: `rjpower`; this diagnostic is not resumable.

The audit, protocol, source ledger, and local gates are in the [pinned logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7810d9e2fd/.agents/logbooks/8054-fa4-sm100.md).

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Waves 7-9: XLA flags and CUDA graphs, plus two fixes to the measurement machinery itself.

## Results

All deltas are in-window against that wave's own `base` arm, which is the adopted configuration (FSDP-sharded small parameters, gate/up interleave ahead of its all-gather, NVLink SHARP). Median `throughput/duration` over steps 5-19; 64 GB200 GPUs; 4.19M tokens/step.

| wave | arm | median | MFU | peak HBM | vs control |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| w7 | base (+`expert_chunks=2`) | 17.008s | 20.57% | 140.8 GiB | — |
| w7 | cudagraphs | 17.202s | 20.34% | 143.8 GiB | −1.14% |
| w7 | combinethresh | 17.581s | 19.90% | 144.9 GiB | −3.37% |
| w7 | epflags | 17.725s | 19.74% | 139.2 GiB | −4.22% |
| w8 | base | 16.570s | 21.12% | 137.2 GiB | — |
| w8 | chunkstack | 17.039s | 20.54% | 140.8 GiB | −2.83% |
| w8 | o1 | 17.182s | 20.36% | 141.3 GiB | −3.70% |
| w9 | base | 16.748s | 20.89% | 137.2 GiB | — |
| w9 | solonly | 16.563s | 21.12% | 137.2 GiB | **+1.10%** |

**Re-enabling CUDA graphs costs 1.14%.** The hero disables command buffers via `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`, with a standing TODO asking whether that is still right. It is: restoring `FUSION,CUSTOM_CALL` is slower and adds 3.0 GiB. At a 17s step the per-launch CPU overhead graphs remove is not on the critical path, and the capture constrains the scheduler.

**The EP hero's scheduler flags cost 4.22% on the FSDP hero.** `--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true` with `--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit=4` is active on `moe_hero_ep` and has never been on the FSDP path. It should stay off: the FSDP step is already 90.3% compute-busy with 5.6% exposed collective, so there is little to hide and the added overlap pressure reorders work that was already well packed.

**Raising collective combine thresholds to 512 MB costs 3.37%** and adds 4.1 GiB. Larger fused collectives delay the first byte and coarsen overlap granularity.

**`--xla_gpu_experimental_autotune_cache_mode=1` (`o1`) costs 3.70%.**

**`expert_chunks=2` does not survive stacking.** It measured +1.63% on the unmodified hero in wave 5, but −2.83% on top of the adopted configuration (wave 8, in-window). Rejected. The full curve on the unmodified hero: 1 → −4.33%, 2 → +1.63%, 4 → baseline, 8 → −2.91%.

**The analytical SOL latency estimator gives +1.10%** (`--xla_gpu_enable_analytical_sol_latency_estimator=true`). This is the only positive result since wave 5. It is also close enough to the measured control-to-control drift (~1.3%) that one reading does not settle it, so wave 10 re-runs it in a fresh window against a fresh control.

## Two fixes to the harness

**A dead flag name took down a 16-node gang.** Wave 9's fusion arm shipped `--xla_gpu_cudnn_gemm_fusion`, `--xla_gpu_enable_custom_fusions`, and `--xla_gpu_enable_address_computation_fusion`; XLA 0.11 has none of them and aborts on an unknown flag. Grepping `libjax_common.so` had reported all three present, because a substring search matches `xla_gpu_cudnn_gemm_fusion` against the real `xla_gpu_cudnn_gemm_fusion_level`.

The preflight now hands each arm's exact `XLA_FLAGS` string to a CPU `jax` subprocess and gates on its exit status. Gating on the abort rather than on one of its messages also catches ill-typed values, which is the other half of this failure: `cudnn_gemm_fusion_level` is an int and rejects `true`. The successor to `enable_address_computation_fusion` is `enable_dynamic_slice_fusion`, already on by default.

**Scoring silently referenced the wrong arm.** The scorer looked for an arm named `control` and fell back to the fastest arm when it found none. Waves 6 onward name the in-window baseline `base`, so every one of those waves hit the fallback. Waves 6-8 are unaffected because their control was also their fastest arm; wave 9 is where it mattered, and `solonly` reads +1.10% rather than a spurious 0 once referenced correctly. The reference is now an explicit tag set and scoring fails loudly if a wave has neither.

## Measurement validity

A large share of launches in this window die before step 0 to the Iris gang-retry generation overlap ([#7650](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7650)) — tasks from one generation connect to a previous generation's JAX coordinator on the fixed port 8476. Wave 9's `userbuffers` arm lost its gang this way, as did the `thd` arms of the FA4 subseries in this same issue. This is not bad hardware: failures rotate across placements, every placement also runs clean siblings, and all 204 nodes are Ready with no faults ([investigation](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/96)). Fixes exist in #7651 and #7994, neither in the deployed controller. The effect on this sweep is lost racks and reruns, not corrupted numbers.

## Wave 10, running

`base`, `solonly` (confirmation), `cudnnfusion` (`--xla_gpu_cudnn_gemm_fusion_level=2`, the corrected fusion lever, aimed at the 5.00 s/step of memory-bound elementwise fusions), `userbuffers` (rerun).

Wave 11 queued: `ceautotune` (`LEVANTER_PALLAS_CE_AUTOTUNE_ON_MISS=1`) and `blockfusion` (`--xla_gpu_experimental_enable_fusion_block_level_rewriter=true`).

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Correction to the previous comment: the `o1` arm sets `JAX_OPTIMIZATION_LEVEL=O1`, not an XLA autotune cache mode. Its −3.70% is the cost of the whole O1 bundle.

That reads more usefully alongside wave 9. O1 bundles the analytical SOL latency estimator, which on its own measured **+1.10%**. So the estimator helps and the rest of the bundle more than undoes it — worth knowing before anyone reaches for O1 as a shortcut to the estimator.

Separately, `--xla_gpu_experimental_autotune_cache_mode` is not settable through `XLA_FLAGS` in XLA 0.11: the name resolves but no value form is accepted. The new preflight gate caught this before launch, along with an out-of-range value in the same arm.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wave 10 reverses wave 9, and that sets a floor under everything measured here.

## The SOL latency estimator does not reproduce

| wave | `base` | `solonly` | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| w9 | 16.748s | 16.563s | **+1.10%** |
| w10 | 16.535s | 16.747s | **−1.28%** |

The two arms swapped places. Both `solonly` readings (16.563, 16.747) fall inside the range spanned by identical-configuration controls (16.535, 16.570, 16.748). Mean `solonly` 16.655s against mean `base` 16.618s. **Rejected — no measurable effect.**

This is what the confirmation arm was for, and it is the reason wave 10 spent a rack re-running a result rather than testing something new.

## The noise floor, measured

Three `base` arms in waves 8-10 ran byte-identical configurations on the same cluster and produced 16.535s, 16.570s, 16.748s: **1.29% peak-to-peak, 0.69% standard deviation.** Within-window MAD is far smaller (0.015-0.057s, under 0.35%), so the variance is between racks, not within a run — placement, not measurement.

The practical consequence: **a single in-window reading cannot resolve an effect below roughly 1.3%.** Several results already reported here sit under that line and should be read as "no measurable effect", not as small wins or small losses:

| result | reported | now |
|---|---|---|
| `NCCL_ALGO=NVLS,Ring` | +0.68% | below floor |
| `NCCL_PROTO=Simple` | +0.19% | below floor |
| CE token block 1024 → 8192 | −0.02% | below floor |
| `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` 0.88 / 0.93 | ~0 / −0.43% | below floor, and consistent with the no-op conclusion |
| `cudagraphs` | −1.14% | marginal, at the floor |
| `interleave_before_gather` alone | +1.54% | marginal, just above the floor |

**The headline is unaffected.** The adopted configuration was measured end to end against a same-window control twice, at +7.85% and +9.08%, both far above the floor. What weakens is the attribution of individual components: `shardsmall` at +2.73% stands on its own, the interleave at +1.54% is marginal alone, and the NVLS setting is not separately established. Every rejection larger than 2% also stands.

I should have established this floor before reading sub-1% arms as directional. It is now in the harness notes so later waves size their arms against it.

## Also in wave 10

**`--xla_gpu_cudnn_gemm_fusion_level=2` costs 3.93%** and adds 0.8 GiB. This was the corrected form of the arm that died on dead flag names. Letting cuDNN take GEMM epilogues was the most direct lever at the 5.00 s/step of memory-bound fusions the profile shows, and it loses cleanly — well outside the noise floor. Rejected.

**`userbuffers` has now lost three racks to [#7650](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7650)** without producing a single step. Each attempt crashes in bootstrap with the gang split across two JAX coordinators — this run had tasks connecting to `10.186.211.189:8476` and `10.186.207.83:8476` at the same time. Zero-copy NCCL collectives are unmeasured, and will stay that way on this controller build. Not an arm result; an infrastructure blocker.

## Wave 11, running

`base`, `ceautotune` (`LEVANTER_PALLAS_CE_AUTOTUNE_ON_MISS=1`), `blockfusion` (the block-level Triton fusion emitter), and `exhaustive` (`--xla_gpu_exhaustive_tiling_search=true --xla_gpu_autotune_level=5` — the "turn autotuning up as far as it goes" item; compile time is paid before the scored window opens).

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wave 11 closes the sweep with four more rejections, and the flag-level search space is now exhausted.


One rack of GB200 (16 nodes × 4 GPUs = 64 GPUs, `cw-us-east-08a`), 300B-class MoE at batch 1024 ×
seq 4096 = 4.19M tokens/step. Eleven waves, 40 arms, every one measured against a control launched
in the same window.

## Result

A configuration change with no effect on numerics takes the hero from **19.37% to 21.30% MFU** —
**+1.93 points, a 9.08% throughput gain** — measured end to end against a same-window control, and
reproduced in a second window at +7.85%. Three components: FSDP-shard the small parameters, move the
MoE gate/up interleave ahead of its all-gather, and select NVLink SHARP for collectives.

That is the entire measured win from the sweep. Of 40 arms, one configuration is adopted, one
component is separately established, and everything else is either a loss or below the noise floor.
The flag-level search space is now exhausted; what remains is structural and is listed at the end.

## Validation approach

Single-arm step time drifts more between cluster windows than most of the effects under test, so
before-and-after comparison across launches is not sound. The protocol that follows:

- **Four arms per wave, launched together, one an unmodified control.** An arm counts only if it
  beats its own wave's control.
- **Median of `throughput/duration` over steps 5-19.** Steps 0-1 are compile and the PGLE recompile;
  steps 2-4 absorb the one-time first-batch data-loader stall. The steady-state distribution is
  right-skewed, so median rather than mean, with MAD reported alongside.
- **Never sum deltas across waves.** The combined arm was measured as a single arm against its own
  control, not inferred from its parts.
- **Report peak HBM per step**, since peak sits pinned against the rematerialization floor and is a
  leading indicator for step time.

### The noise floor, and what it retires

Four `base` arms across waves 8-11 ran byte-identical configurations on the same cluster:

| w8 | w9 | w10 | w11 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16.570s | 16.748s | 16.535s | 16.639s |

**1.28% peak-to-peak, 0.57% standard deviation.** Within-window MAD is 0.015-0.057s (under 0.35%),
so the variance is between racks, not within a run — placement, not measurement.

A single in-window reading therefore cannot resolve an effect below roughly 1.3%. This was
established late, in wave 10, by an arm that reversed sign between waves. Applying it retroactively
retires six readings previously reported as small effects:

| result | reported | corrected reading |
|---|---|---|
| SOL latency estimator | +1.10% (w9) | **−1.28% (w10)** — reverses; no effect |
| `NCCL_ALGO=NVLS,Ring` | +0.68% | below floor |
| `NCCL_PROTO=Simple` | +0.19% | below floor |
| CE token block 1024 → 8192 | −0.02% | below floor |
| `MEM_FRACTION` 0.88 / 0.93 | ~0 / −0.43% | below floor; consistent with the no-op conclusion |
| CE autotune on miss | +0.26% | below floor |

The headline is unaffected: +9.08% and +7.85% are far outside the floor, and both are end-to-end
measurements against same-window controls rather than sums of parts. What weakens is per-component
attribution — `shardsmall` at +2.73% stands alone, the interleave at +1.54% is marginal alone, and
the NVLS setting is not separately established.

### Three gates in front of a launch

Iris ships the local worktree, so all four racks in a wave run one code state and a single mistake
takes down the control along with the arms. Each gate below covers a failure that had already cost
four racks:

- **`sweep_preflight.py`** traces every arm through `next_token_loss` and its gradient on CPU under
  `jax.eval_shape`, at a 2-layer shape, through the same `apply_hero_overrides` path the launcher
  uses. An attribute typo in the cross-entropy config plumbing had killed a whole wave at step 0.
- **`XLA_FLAGS` go to XLA's own parser.** Each arm's exact flag string runs in a CPU `jax`
  subprocess and is gated on exit status. Wave 9 lost a 16-node gang because all three flag names in
  its fusion arm are absent from XLA 0.11; grepping `libjax_common.so` had reported them present,
  because a substring search matches `xla_gpu_cudnn_gemm_fusion` against the real
  `xla_gpu_cudnn_gemm_fusion_level`. Gating on the abort rather than on one of its messages also
  catches ill-typed values, which is the other half of that failure — `cudnn_gemm_fusion_level` is
  an int and rejects `true`. The gate has since caught a second rack-killer, an unsettable value for
  `xla_gpu_experimental_autotune_cache_mode`.
- **An empty `WANDB_API_KEY`** satisfies a plain environment lookup and then fails six minutes later
  inside `trainer.initialize()`, on every rack at once. W&B also refuses to re-initialize a run id a
  crashed attempt already claimed.

Scoring had its own defect: it looked for an arm named `control` and silently fell back to the
fastest arm when it found none. Waves 6 onward name the baseline `base`, so every one hit the
fallback. Waves 6-8 were unaffected because their control was also fastest; wave 9 is where it
mattered. The reference is now an explicit tag set and scoring fails loudly if a wave has neither.

## Everything tested

Deltas are against each arm's own wave control. Anything inside ±1.3% is below the floor.

| Change | Delta | Peak HBM | Verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Combined** (three below) | **+9.08%**, +1.93 pts | 137.2 GiB | **adopt** |
| FSDP-shard small parameters | +2.73% | 148.9 GiB | adopt |
| Interleave before gather | +1.54% | — | adopt (marginal alone) |
| `NCCL_ALGO=NVLS,Ring` | +0.68% | — | keep; below floor alone |
| CE autotune on miss | +0.26% | 137.2 GiB | below floor |
| `NCCL_PROTO=Simple` | +0.19% | — | below floor |
| CE token block 1024 → 8192 | −0.02% | +9.1 GiB | below floor |
| `MEM_FRACTION` 0.88 / 0.93 | ~0 / −0.43% | 137.2 GiB | **keep as a lever** |
| SOL latency estimator | +1.10% then −1.28% | 137.2 GiB | reject (does not reproduce) |
| Re-enable CUDA graphs | −1.14% | +3.0 GiB | reject |
| `NCCL_PROTO=LL128` | −2.70% | — | reject |
| `expert_chunks` 4 → 8 | −2.91% | +3.3 GiB | reject |
| `expert_chunks` 4 → 2, stacked | −2.83% | 140.8 GiB | reject |
| Collective combine → 512 MB | −3.37% | +4.1 GiB | reject |
| `JAX_OPTIMIZATION_LEVEL=O1` | −3.70% | 141.3 GiB | reject |
| `cudnn_gemm_fusion_level=2` | −3.93% | 138.0 GiB | reject |
| EP hero's scheduler flags | −4.22% | 139.2 GiB | reject |
| `expert_chunks` 4 → 1 | −4.33% | 152.8 GiB | reject |
| Exhaustive tiling + autotune 5 | −4.50% | 145.3 GiB | reject |
| Block-level fusion emitter | **−60.61%** | 137.2 GiB | reject |
| `remat_mode="save_moe"` | device OOM | 386.7 GiB requested | infeasible |
| `remat_mode="offload_moe"` | host OOM | 144.0 GiB pinned host | infeasible |
| NCCL user buffers | — | — | unmeasurable (3 racks lost to #7650) |

`expert_chunks=2` deserves a note: it measured +1.63% on the unmodified hero, then −2.83% stacked on
the adopted configuration in a fresh window. Effects here are not independent, which is why the
combined arm is measured end to end rather than assembled from components.

### The two adopted code changes

`small_param_sharding="fsdp"` was ranked 6th before measurement and is the largest single win. The
profile showed 0.69 s/step of per-layer all-reduce on parameters small enough that replication looked
free. It is not free: each replicated parameter's gradient is its own collective, and 48 layers ×
several parameters is a long tail of small launches that neither fills the link nor overlaps well.
Sharding one dimension of each folds those gradients into the existing reduce-scatter.

`interleave_before_gather` is a two-line change whose output is bitwise identical. The chunked
`sonic_cute` gate/up interleave runs on the *gathered* chunk; the interleave is along the last axis
and the all-gather along axis 1, so they commute, and doing it on the local shard first touches 1/64
of the elements. The profile priced this region at 0.555 s/step.

The two together are worth more than the sum of their separate measurements. An earlier draft
attributed this to freed HBM buying back rematerialization; wave 6 falsified that. `shardsmall`
alone *raises* peak HBM to 148.9 GiB and is still the largest single win. The superadditivity
reproduces; its cause is open, and some of the apparent magnitude is control drift now that the
floor is known.

### Memory: keep the allocator fraction as a lever

`XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` is never set, so JAX's 0.75 default offers 138.22 GiB of the
roughly 184.3 GiB on the part. Raising it to 0.88 and 0.93 moved the limit to 162.18 and 171.40 GiB,
confirmed in per-step `memory/limit_gib`, and changed nothing: peak stayed at 137.21 GiB.

It is a no-op today because nothing consumes the memory, not because the memory is unavailable. The
hero's recompute comes from an explicit `remat_mode="recompute_all"` `jax.checkpoint` policy fixed at
trace time. XLA's `HloRematerialization` pass — the one that responds to the allocator limit —
engages only when peak exceeds it: true of the old control at 140.90 GiB against 138.22 GiB, false
of the adopted configuration at 137.21 GiB.

**This stays in the configuration as a lever, not a rejected arm.** Every future change that trades
memory for time needs the ceiling raised first, and both 0.88 and 0.93 are proven safe on this
hardware, including against NCCL and cuBLAS workspaces outside the pool. Pair it with whatever
finally spends the memory rather than testing it alone again.

### Both memory strategies are blocked, for different reasons

Activation offloading ranked first before measurement, on 5.09 s/step (28% of the step) of backward
recompute. Both routes are blocked at this shape:

- **`save_moe` is device-bound.** It requests 386.7 GiB against a 138.22 GiB limit. On the FSDP
  `sonic_cute` path two tags are live across all 48 layers — dispatch input and dispatch output — at
  roughly 155 GB each.
- **`offload_moe` is host-bound.** Narrowed to the one tag worth its C2C traffic, it needs a
  144.00 GiB pinned-host arena and `xla_gpu_host_bfc` cannot get it. A rank has roughly 212 GiB of
  Grace LPDDR and the offloaded optimizer state already holds a large share.

Offloading a subset of layers would fit, and is not expressible: all 48 layers run under one
`jax.scan` with a single remat policy. That makes breaking the scan the blocker for the highest-value
remaining item.

## Two corrections to the pre-sweep analysis

**The step model was wrong, and the correction changes which candidates matter.** Summing xprof
`hlo_stats` self-times and attributing the remainder to a bubble double-counts across concurrent
streams. Taking the union of the XPlane timeline instead, per 18.0 s step: the compute stream is busy
16.28 s (90.3%), a collective runs alone for 1.02 s (5.6%), and the device is fully idle 0.49 s
(2.7%). A kernel is resident 97.0-97.3% of the capture. There is no 3.17 s bubble and no 23.6%
"perfect overlap" ceiling. 77% of collective time already overlaps compute, and on a GPU that overlap
is SM contention rather than free execution.

This is why every candidate about hiding collectives behind compute failed, and why the only measured
wins **delete work from the compute stream**.

**PGLE has never worked on this cluster.** Every run logs `PGLE collected an empty trace ... contention
with another tool that subscribes to CUPTI`, twice per process across all 16 processes, with no
profiler attached. Nothing in the training code starts a trace, so the CUPTI subscriber is node-level.
XLA's latency-hiding scheduler has been running on static cost estimates throughout. An earlier
"PGLE worth at most 0.22 MFU" compared broken PGLE against no PGLE and should be disregarded.

## The seventeen candidates, assessed

| # | Candidate | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | MoE execution bubbles | No bubble to recover — 90.3% compute-busy, 2.7% idle. Deprioritized on evidence. |
| 2 | Break the 1-layer `jax.scan` | **Top remaining item**, on different grounds than proposed: not overlap, but per-layer remat policy. |
| 3 | Fusing kernels | 5.00 s/step of memory-bound fusions is real. The largest named offender was the interleave, now adopted. Both XLA fusion levers lose: cuDNN epilogues −3.93%, block-level emitter −60.61%. |
| 4 | Increasing available HBM | Per-step HBM telemetry added; the memory is available and unused. A lever, not a win. |
| 5 | Stronger offloading | Infeasible at this shape both ways; blocked behind #2. |
| 6 | Better sharding | **+2.73%, the largest single win.** Adopted. |
| 7 | Improving SConv | Untested — needs a kernel, not a flag. |
| 8 | Comms protocol | NVLS kept but below floor; LL128 −2.70%; Simple below floor. Smaller than estimated because there is no exposed bubble. |
| 9 | Faster Muon | Untested. |
| 10 | Better MoE chunking | Measured across 1/2/4/8. Default 4 is best once stacked; the curve is non-monotonic and non-independent. |
| 11 | Parameter banks | Untested. The interleave result is direct evidence this category pays. |
| 12 | Cross-entropy kernel | Tiling flat, autotune-on-miss below floor. There is **no GPU Pallas CE kernel** — `pallas_tpu` is TPU-only; GPU has `xla`, `batched_xla`, `reference`. A rewrite is untested. |
| 13 | Is FA4 optimal? | 1.27 s at 211 TF/s, 8% of peak. A separate subseries comparing the segmented fork against native SM100 THD lost its arms to #7650 and is unresolved. |
| 14 | Is the MoE kernel optimal? | Weight-gradient kernel 1.50 s at 947 TF/s, 38% of peak. Untested. |
| 15 | Different JAX flags | **Ten arms, zero wins.** Every flag tested is neutral or worse. |
| 16 | Other inefficiencies | Found the two adopted wins here. |
| 17 | Extreme autotune | **−4.50%.** Exhaustive tiling search at autotune level 5 is worse, and PGLE — the mechanism this item hoped to strengthen — has never run at all. |

## What is still open

1. **Break the 1-layer `jax.scan`.** No longer an overlap argument. It is the blocker for per-layer
   remat policy, the only route to the 5.09 s/step of recompute now that both whole-model memory
   strategies are ruled out, and the only way to spend the ~46 GiB of headroom.
2. **FA4 and the MoE weight-gradient kernel.** 8% and 38% of peak. These delete compute-stream work,
   the only category that has paid.
3. **Parameter banks (QKV in one parameter).** Same category; the interleave result is evidence for it.
4. **Fix the node-level CUPTI conflict so PGLE can run at all.** Unmeasured on this cluster; the
   scheduler is running blind.
5. **Land the #7650 fixes** (#7651, #7994, neither in the deployed controller). Four racks were lost
   to gang-retry coordinator overlap during this sweep, and one arm is permanently unmeasured.

Deprioritized by measurement: MoE all-gather pipelining and the overlap case for breaking the scan
(no bubble), cross-entropy tiling (flat), MoE chunk counts (worse), NCCL protocol beyond NVLS (below
floor), XLA fusion flags (worse), and autotune escalation (worse).

## Artifacts and reproduction

- [XProf trace, steps 10-12](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fgprof-xprof-1rack-20260807)

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wave 12 decomposes `JAX_OPTIMIZATION_LEVEL=O1`, and the result corrects what I wrote about it two comments ago.

O1 is a documented bundle ([NVIDIA JAX toolbox](https://docs.nvidia.com/jax-toolbox/performance-profiling/gpu-performance)): latency hiding scheduler, collective pipelining (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter), the unified SOL latency estimator, and while-loop double buffering. I had described its −3.70% as "the estimator helps and the rest of the bundle more than undoes it." That was unsupported — three of the four components had never been measured.

| arm | contents | delta |
|---|---|---|
| `base` | adopted configuration | — |
| `pipelined` | the three pipelining flags | **−2.35%** |
| `o1nolhs` | pipelining + SOL + double buffering | **−7.06%** |
| `doublebuffer` | double buffering alone | still compiling |

**Removing the latency hiding scheduler from O1 makes it worse, not better.** Full O1 is −3.70%; O1 without LHS is −7.06%. Yet LHS measured −4.22% on its own in the `epflags` arm. The components interact strongly, and the earlier reading of LHS as simply bad was context-dependent.

The mechanism is consistent across all four measurements: pipelined collectives need a latency-hiding scheduler to overlap them with anything. Without LHS, pipelining is added scheduling structure with nothing hiding behind it, which is what `pipelined` alone (−2.35%) shows directly, and what makes `o1nolhs` the worst arm of the wave.

This is the same story the profile told at the start. The step is 90.3% compute-busy with 2.7% idle and 5.6% exposed collective. There is almost nothing for latency-hiding machinery to recover, so every mechanism in this family — LHS, pipelining, the O1 bundle, larger combine thresholds, the EP hero's scheduler flags — costs more in scheduling than it wins in overlap. That is now measured six ways rather than argued once.

**Double buffering costs roughly 6× compile time.** Its first compile took about 22 minutes against 3.5 for the control, which is a real operational cost independent of whatever step time it lands at. It unrolls the 48-layer `jax.scan` twice, so the graph doubles. Step numbers to follow.

## Corrections carried forward

- `--xla_gpu_enable_address_computation_fusion` does not exist in XLA 0.11. Its successor `--xla_gpu_enable_dynamic_slice_fusion` **defaults to false**, so it is untested rather than already on, contrary to what I wrote in the wave 7-9 comment. It is running now as wave 13's `dsfusion`.
- `--xla_gpu_lhs_enable_gpu_async_tracker` does not exist in this build.
- Combine thresholds: one layer's FSDP shard is 231 MB, so the usual "size it to one transformer layer" rule was already satisfied by the 512 MB arm that measured −3.37%. Nothing can merge across `jax.scan` iterations whatever the threshold, so wave 13 tests 8 GB standalone and wave 14 pairs it with the unroll that finally gives it two layers of collectives to combine.

## Infrastructure

[#7994](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7994) is cherry-picked onto this branch. It is client-side — it changes only `iris/runtime/jax_init.py`, which ships with the worktree — so it takes effect without a controller redeploy. Rank 0 now asks the kernel for a free coordinator port and publishes it through endpoint discovery instead of every generation binding 8476.

Wave 13 is the first launch carrying it, and includes a fourth attempt at `userbuffers`, which lost three racks to this failure mode without reaching step 0.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Wave 13.** Two more rejections, both well outside the ±1.57% resolution of a single reading.

| arm | delta | peak HBM |
|---|---|---|
| `base` | — | 137.2 GiB |
| `dsfusion` (`--xla_gpu_enable_dynamic_slice_fusion=true`) | **−6.13%** | 148.8 GiB |
| `combine8g` (8 GB AG/RS/AR combine thresholds) | **−13.48%** | 139.1 GiB |

`dsfusion` is the successor to the `address_computation_fusion` flag I had wrongly written off as already-on; it defaults to false and it costs 6% plus 11.6 GiB of peak. `combine8g` is the worst collective result of the sweep and confirms the reasoning behind it: one layer's FSDP shard is 231 MB, all 48 layers sit inside a single `jax.scan`, and nothing can merge across scan iterations, so an 8 GB threshold only delays first-byte on collectives it cannot combine.

**`userbuffers` is dropped after four attempts.** The fourth ran with [#7994](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7994) cherry-picked and a kernel-selected coordinator port (61601), and still lost its coordination service, while every sibling arm in all four waves survived. The failure is arm-correlated, not the fixed-port collision — so my earlier attribution of the first three losses to #7650 was probably wrong. It is a zero-copy collective optimization on a workload that is 90.3% compute-busy, so it is not worth a fifth rack.

**The remaining collective arms are retired unrun** — pipelined P2P, and the combine threshold paired with an unroll. Seven independent measurements now agree that latency-hiding and collective-combining machinery has nothing to recover on this step: the scheduler alone (−4.22%), collective pipelining (−2.35%), the O1 bundle (−3.70%), O1 without its scheduler (−7.06%), 512 MB combine (−3.37%), 8 GB combine (−13.48%), and NCCL user buffers (unmeasurable).

**Wave 14 is running** and is the last experimental wave: the scan unroll rerun, and two batch sizes that finally spend the HBM headroom. Batch arms do more work per step, so scoring switches to tokens/s automatically.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Wave 14.** The first positive result since the adopted configuration, and the flag search ends.

| arm | batch | median | Mtok/s | MFU | peak HBM | vs control |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `base` | 1024 | 16.667s | 0.252 | 20.99% | 137.2 GiB | — |
| `batch1152` | 1152 | 18.427s | 0.256 | 21.36% | 153.1 GiB | **+1.76%** |

**Spending the HBM headroom on batch size works.** Step time rises as it should for 12.5% more work per step, and throughput rises more. Scoring switches to tokens/s here because step time stops being comparable once arms process different token counts.

Peak lands at 153.1 GiB, well past the 138.22 GiB the default allocator fraction offers, so `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.88` is load-bearing rather than incidental. That is the memory lever paying off exactly as argued when it measured as a no-op on its own: it was never a win by itself, it was a precondition waiting for something to spend the memory.

At +1.76% against the ±1.57% resolution of a single reading this is real but marginal, which the wrap-up wave settles over 40 scored steps.

**`doublebuffer` is dropped after two attempts**, both ending in `rendezvous.cc` timeouts with ranks waiting on each other. The mechanism is consistent: unrolling the 48-layer `jax.scan` makes compilation both slow (22 minutes against the control's 3.5) and skewed across ranks, so the gang times out waiting on itself before reaching step 0.

That is worth recording as a result rather than a failure. Breaking the scan is the top structural item in this sweep, and the cheapest approximation of it — letting XLA double-buffer the loop — is not merely unprofitable but does not compile at this scale. A real attempt needs selective unrolling with compile time treated as a first-class constraint, not a flag.

**`batch1280` did not produce a window** and is not being retried; `batch1152` already establishes the effect.

## Wrap-up wave, running

45 steps, 40 scored, on the merged main. Note that main moves the hero to one process per GPU (`HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK` 1 → 4), so these absolute numbers are not continuous with waves 1-14; the in-window control is what the deltas rest on.

- `control` — the hero as it was before this sweep
- `control2` — byte-identical to `control`
- `adopted` — FSDP-sharded small parameters, interleave before gather, NVLink SHARP
- `adoptedbatch` — the above plus batch 1152 at `MEM_FRACTION=0.88`

`control2` earns its rack. Every arm in a wave lands on a different rack, so placement variance has been confounded with the effect under test throughout this sweep; the 1.28% figure comes from four controls spread across waves and therefore also carries drift over time. Two identical controls in one window isolate placement alone, and that is the number every delta in the final report should be read against.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Wave `final2` — wrap-up measurement, and why `adoptedbatch` kept dying**

45 steps per arm, 40 scored, all four racks in one window at production priority.

| arm | n | batch | median step | Mtok/s | MFU | peak HBM | vs control |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `adopted` | 40 | 1024 | 17.542 s | 0.239 | 19.95% | 146.0 GiB | **+2.87%** |
| `control2` | 40 | 1024 | 17.919 s | 0.234 | 19.53% | 141.2 GiB | +0.78% |
| `control` | 40 | 1024 | 18.060 s | 0.232 | 19.37% | 141.2 GiB | — |
| `adoptedbatch` | — | 1152 | crashed at step 4 | | | | |

`control2` is byte-identical to `control`. The 0.78% between them is the first clean
measurement of placement variance in this sweep — earlier replicates were separated in time,
so drift and placement were confounded. It sets the floor a single paired reading can resolve.

Pooling `final` and `final2`, `adopted` beats `control` by **+3.31%, 95% CI [+2.60%, +4.01%]**
(3 control readings, 2 adopted, 40 scored steps each, post-merge with `main`).

**`adoptedbatch` (batch 1152) is a hard HBM out-of-memory, in both attempts and at both ceilings.**
It cost three runs to see because the error does not appear where you would look for it. Fifteen
of sixteen ranks report only this:

```
E coordination_service.cc:1520] Shutdown barrier in coordination service has failed
F client.h:80] Terminating process because the JAX distributed service detected fatal errors
```

with no traceback, five minutes after their last line. One rank has the actual cause:

```
CU_MEMPOOL_ATTR_USED_MEM_HIGH: 184037715581     # 171.4 GiB — the entire 0.93 ceiling
jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory while trying to
  allocate 131.94GiB. [executable_name='jit_train_step']
```

The five minutes is the JAX shutdown-barrier timeout; the surviving ranks are waiting on a peer
that already exited. Reading only the loudest ranks gives an infrastructure story. It is not one.

The two ceilings fail differently, which confirms the diagnosis rather than muddying it. At 0.88
(162.2 GiB) batch 1152 peaks at 155.8 GiB and *runs*, but at 40 s/step against its siblings' 17 —
`HloRematerialization` responds to allocator pressure by buying memory with recompute. Raising to
0.93 removes that pressure, so steps 0–4 run at a healthy 19 s, and the peak that remat was
suppressing now arrives in full and does not fit. Note the pool state at the failure: 167.4 GiB
reserved against 25.7 GiB live, so the 131.94 GiB request dies on fragmentation, not on a gradual
climb in working set.

Batch 1088 (+6.25% tokens) is the remaining untested point and is running now as wave `final3`,
paired in-window against the adopted config at 1024 under the same 0.93 ceiling. 6.25% clears the
0.78% placement variance by enough that one paired reading settles it.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Correction to my previous comment: the step-4 crash is caused by the allocator ceiling, not by batch 1152.**

Wave `final3` launched two arms at `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.93`: batch 1088, and a **batch
1024** control. The batch-1024 control crashed at step 4 with the same failure I had attributed to
the larger batch:

```
gpu_async_0 cuMemAllocAsync failed to allocate 131108848800 bytes: CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY
CU_MEMPOOL_ATTR_USED_MEM_HIGH: 184037715581      # 171.4 GiB — the 0.93 ceiling
jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory while trying to
  allocate 122.10GiB. [executable_name='jit_train_step']
```

Batch 1024 is the shape that ran 40 clean steps in `final2`. The controlled comparison is exact —
same commit, same batch, same arm configuration, differing only in the allocator fraction:

| arm | batch | `MEM_FRACTION` | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `final2-adopted` | 1024 | 0.75 (default) | 40 scored steps, 17.542 s |
| `final3-control` | 1024 | **0.93** | **OOM at step 4** |
| `final2-adoptedbatch` | 1152 | 0.93 | OOM at step 4 |
| `final-adoptedbatch` | 1152 | 0.88 | runs, 40 s/step |

So the necessary condition is the 0.93 ceiling on merged `main`, and batch size only scales the
failing request (122.10 GiB at 1024, 131.94 GiB at 1152).

The mechanism is the opposite of the one I described. XLA sizes the `jit_train_step` temp buffer to
the allocator limit it is given. At 0.93 it plans a single ~122 GiB slab that cannot coexist with
resident parameters and optimizer state, and the run dies on the first step that needs the whole
buffer. At 0.88 it plans a smaller buffer that does fit, which is why batch 1152 ran there — slowly,
at 40 s/step, because the tighter budget makes `HloRematerialization` buy memory with recompute. The
0.75 default is the only ceiling proven stable on merged `main`.

Two consequences:

- **`MEM_FRACTION=0.93` is not safe on merged `main`,** though it was measured safe pre-merge (wave 6,
  16.637 s, no failure). That is a second regression across the merge, alongside the adopted config
  losing 64% of its win. Raising this ceiling was listed in the report as a proven-safe lever; it is
  not one on current `main`, and the report is corrected.
- **The batch-size result is unresolved on merged `main`.** Batch 1152's only positive reading
  (+1.76%) is pre-merge. Post-merge, every ceiling that fits forces enough rematerialization to lose
  more than the extra tokens gain. Relaunching batch 1088 at 0.88.

What made this expensive to see: 15 of 16 ranks report only `Shutdown barrier in coordination service
has failed` with no traceback, five minutes (the JAX shutdown-barrier timeout) after their last line,
because they are waiting on a peer that already exited. Only the rank that raised carries the cause.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **The sweep's actual mechanism, found in the last wave: peak HBM against the allocator limit.**

Wave `final4` held the ceiling at 0.88 and varied only the batch. Its batch-1024 control failed too —
with the **same 122.10 GiB request** as the 0.93 arm:

```
gpu_async_3 cuMemAllocAsync failed to allocate 131108848800 bytes: CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY
CU_MEMPOOL_ATTR_USED_MEM_HIGH: 174143212460      # 162.2 GiB — the 0.88 ceiling
jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory while trying to
  allocate 122.10GiB. [executable_name='jit_train_step']
```

An identical request at two different ceilings means the allocation is a fixed requirement of the
program, not something sized to the limit. That sent me back to the per-step memory telemetry, and
every arm in the sweep falls cleanly on one side of a single threshold:

| run | batch | peak | limit | `HloRematerialization` | step |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| `w5-control` (pre-merge) | 1024 | 140.90 | 138.22 | **on** | 18.067 s |
| `w5-combined` (pre-merge adopted) | 1024 | **137.21** | 138.22 | **off** | **16.426 s** |
| `w6-memfrac88` | 1024 | 137.21 | 162.18 | off | 16.565 s |
| `w6-memfrac93` | 1024 | 137.21 | 171.40 | off | 16.637 s |
| `w14-batch1152` | 1152 | 153.14 | 162.18 | off | 18.427 s |
| `final2-control` (merged) | 1024 | 141.24 | 138.22 | on | 18.060 s |
| `final2-adopted` (merged) | 1024 | **146.00** | 138.22 | **on** | 17.542 s |

XLA's `HloRematerialization` engages only when peak exceeds the allocator limit, and pays for the
excess in recompute. So:

**The +9.08% headline was, mechanically, 3.69 GiB.** The adopted configuration took peak from 140.90
to 137.21 GiB, crossed under the 138.22 GiB default, and switched rematerialization off. That is why
its two components are superadditive — neither crosses the threshold alone, and together they do.

**It explains the merge regression exactly.** `main`'s one-process-per-GPU change added 8.79 GiB to
the adopted configuration's peak, 137.21 → 146.00, putting it back above the limit. Both arms now
rematerialize, the adopted configuration keeps only its direct compute savings, and the win falls
from +9.08% to +3.31%.

**And it corrects this report.** I previously wrote that wave 6 falsified the "freed HBM buys back
rematerialization" theory, because raising the ceiling to 0.88/0.93 changed nothing. It changed
nothing because the adopted configuration was *already below* the limit at 0.75 — precisely what the
theory predicts. Wave 6 is consistent with the mechanism, not against it. That was the wrong call and
it cost several waves of looking in the wrong place.

The obvious recovery — raise the ceiling, escape remat — is blocked on merged `main`: any ceiling
high enough to switch the pass off exposes that 122.10 GiB allocation, which the pool cannot serve at
0.88 or 0.93. The hero currently runs *because* it is rematerializing. Batch 1152 at 0.88 is the
exception that shows the rule: its 153.14 GiB peak keeps remat engaged, so it runs, at 40 s/step.

**This makes the top open item concrete and small.** Recovering 8.79 GiB of post-merge peak is worth
+5.8 points of step time and is a far more tractable problem than anything else remaining on the
list. The alternative route needs the 122.10 GiB `jit_train_step` allocation made serviceable first —
worth checking whether a BFC allocator rather than `cuda_async` serves it, since the failure is a
single-block request against a pool that has already reached the ceiling.

The batch-size question is closed as unresolvable on merged `main`: every ceiling either forces
enough recompute to lose what the extra tokens gain, or OOMs.

Full report: `report-sweep` rev 4.

comments.body:
🤖 The routed-expert mask optimization completed four checkpoint-restored control/treatment pairs on 64 GB200 GPUs. Against main `1f9c387b6c45` plus the native SM100 backward-attention optimization from #9228, throughput increased 1.63% (paired Fieller 95% interval: +0.22% to +3.09%). All 4,096 paired input fingerprints matched, but losses differed at 63 of 64 updates, with a maximum absolute difference of 0.000957 nats; the second run's throughput was 0.53% lower. This single pair establishes observed baseline variation. It does not establish an equivalence margin or explain all loss differences seen in the separate inverse-routing optimization, which replaces inverse-permutation sorts with indexed integer writes. [Repeatability report](https://github.com/mcwitt-agent/marin/blob/8391de52880b9f53067c2c28e6f10c038de4f724/experiments/benchmarks/inverse_routing_repeatability_results.md) and [derived measurements and protocol](https://github.com/mcwitt-agent/marin/blob/8391de52880b9f53067c2c28e6f10c038de4f724/experiments/benchmarks/inverse_routing_repeatability_results.json).

Its original pair 3 remains excluded in full because Iris marked the job failed after a pod disappeared, despite all training subprocesses exiting successfully. One replacement pair has been submitted; the study still requires Iris to record job success before a pair enters the primary estimate.

issues.body:
The weekly fork-migration system from #8048 is in place: a refresh-fork skill and
per-fork descriptors (#8068, #8117), a weekly ferry coordinator (#8245) with Loom
federation (#8284), and automated re-pinning for the vLLM GPU wheel (#8292). The TPU
vLLM stack refreshed to tpu-inference v0.26.0 (#8207) on top of the externalized
stack (#8063), and the GPU wheel now discovers its `_C` extension by shape across the
CUDA 13 / stable-ABI boundary (#8250). This issue tracks the work that remains after
that rollout, and is the canonical fork-migration tracker going forward. It supersedes
#8048 and folds in the refresh trackers #8298, #7097, #7143, and #6480.

1. Promote the Harbor one-time catch-up. marin-community/harbor#73 re-ports the fork
   overlay onto current upstream and folds the standalone `harbor-config` package into
   `harbor.models`. It is mergeable with `marin-precommit`, `marin-style-sync`, and
   `tests` green. Two steps need an admin/reviewer: drop the retired `harbor-config`
   context from the fork `main` branch protection (it no longer reports, so it blocks
   the merge), then review and merge, and promote the caught-up tree to protected
   `main`. Done when fork `main` carries the caught-up overlay and its protection no
   longer requires `harbor-config`.

2. Bump the Marin Harbor pin. After harbor#73 lands, re-pin `config/external/harbor`
   to the landed `main` SHA, migrate the `harbor_config.*` imports in
   `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py` to `harbor.models.*`, and
   keep the migration.toml [harbor] nuances. The aime-smoke e2e already passed
   end-to-end against the catch-up branch on qwen3-0.6b. Closes out the blocker path
   #8298.

3. Migrate MarinSkyRL as a managed Harbor consumer (#7920). The SkyRL fork depends on
   `harbor[analysis,datasets,daytona]` floating on `main` plus the standalone
   `harbor-config` wheel, so the harbor.models fold in harbor#73 breaks any SkyRL
   relock. Pin harbor to an explicit immutable ref, migrate off `harbor-config` to
   `harbor.models`, and give SkyRL a Marin-style update-external plus one terminal-bench
   e2e. Cadence stays decoupled and coordinated on breaking changes rather than weekly
   lockstep. Tracked under #7920.

4. Make the ferry's evalchemy leg observable. The weekly run produced no PR and filed
   no blocker for evalchemy. Confirm whether that is a legitimate no-op (the fork
   already matches upstream `main`) or a silent failure, and have the leg emit an
   explicit no-op summary either way.

5. Publish prebuilt TPU vLLM fork wheels (#7143). Cold TPU jobs still source-build the
   `vllm` and `tpu-inference` forks; a Marin-controlled index would let serve, eval,
   and RL install a pinned wheel. Standalone spec in #7143.

6. Resolve the Marin-owned pin audit (#6480). Decide whether Levanter can move to a
   Transformers 5 range and drop the tpu-inference Gemma4 guard, and keep the
   JAX/libtpu/torch/torchvision alignment documented against the fork stack. The
   descriptor records these as nuances; the decision is open. Spec in #6480.

spillover_issues.author: WhenWen
spillover_issues.body:
Benchmark results for the RMNP optimizer added in #8950, run at the completed 130M
settings from #6301 so the numbers are directly comparable to that submission.

## Summary

RMNP trails a freshly-tuned Muon baseline by **0.032 C4 BPB** at 130M. A 32x
learning-rate sweep places RMNP's optimum at **0.003**, the default already used in
#8950, so the gap is not a matter of LR tuning. Throughput is unaffected: MFU is
flat across the sweep and equal to Muon's.

## Results

All runs: Qwen3 130M, FineWeb-Edu 10B, seq 4096, batch 128, 4959 steps
(2.60B tokens), seed 0, v5p-8 in us-central1. Only the matrix LR varies.

| Run | Matrix LR | C4 BPB | vs Muon | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muon (fresh baseline) | 0.016 | **1.16754** | — | 23.789% |
| #6301 reference | — | 1.16656 | −0.001 | 23.111% |
| RMNP | **0.003** | **1.19958** | **+0.032** | 23.787% |
| RMNP | 0.006 | 1.20263 | +0.035 | 23.575% |
| RMNP | 0.012 | 1.21668 | +0.049 | 23.764% |
| RMNP | 0.024 | 1.22354 | +0.056 | 23.778% |
| RMNP | 0.0015 | 1.22716 | +0.060 | 23.859% |
| RMNP | 0.00075 | 1.27212 | +0.105 | 23.849% |

## Observations

**The LR curve is single-minimum over a 32x range**, with the minimum at the
default 0.003. Tuning does not move the optimum.

**The gap is not LR mis-tuning.** The two best LRs differ by 0.00305 BPB, while the
distance to Muon is 0.03204 — roughly 10x larger.

**No throughput tradeoff.** MFU spans 23.58–23.86% across the sweep and matches
Muon's 23.789%, so the quality gap is not being paid for with speed.

**The baseline is trustworthy.** The fresh Muon run reproduces the #6301 reference
to within 0.001 BPB. This control mattered: both fresh runs reach ~639k tok/s versus
the reference's ~621k, so comparing RMNP's MFU against the archived number alone
would have shown a spurious ~3% speedup attributable to library changes rather than
to the optimizer.

## Caveats

- **One seed per point.** The 0.032 gap to Muon is far outside plausible seed noise,
  but the within-RMNP ordering (e.g. 0.003 vs 0.006, which differ by 0.003 BPB) is
  not resolved by this data.
- **130M only.** #6301 also reports completed 300M and 520M comparisons; whether the
  gap narrows with scale is untested here.
- Four runs took preemptions on preemptible capacity (lr012 three times, lr0015 /
  lr006 / lr024 once each). All resumed from checkpoint with `failures=0` and
  completed the full 4959 steps, so final metrics are unaffected.

## Reproduction

Optimizer implementations taken unchanged from #8950 at `d013891f9`. Each run:

```
python -m experiments.rmnp_speedrun \
  --optimizer {rmnp|muon} --learning-rate <lr> --run-id <id> --run
```

Shared recipe: linear schedule, no warmup, last 80% decay to zero; momentum 0.95
with Nesterov; Adam beta1 0.8 / beta2 0.98, eps 1e-15, Adam LR 0.0032; weight decay
0.1; global grad clip 1.0; bf16 compute with fp32 master params. Muon additionally
uses `muon_epsilon=1e-5`. Evaluation is the full C4 validation cache every 1000
steps and at the end.

W&B runs are in `marin-community/speedrun` under the group
`rmnp-pr8950-qwen3-130m-20260920`.

## Suggested next steps

1. Seed-variance runs at 0.003 and 0.006 to firm up the within-RMNP ordering.
2. Repeat at the 300M / 520M rungs to test whether the gap is scale-dependent.

spillover_issues.author: claude[bot]
spillover_issues.body:
## Problem

Endpoint lease renewal currently reuses the full `RegisterEndpoint` RPC, one call per endpoint per renewal interval (`EndpointLeaseRenewer.tick` → `_renew_one` → `self._register(lease.request)` in [`endpoint_client.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/endpoint_client.py#L274-L296)). Reusing register made the switchover trivial — existing clients always call `register`, so register-or-renew needed no new client surface — but it means each renewal re-sends the entire registration payload and does a full register's worth of work server-side.

With many endpoints per task this is more expensive than it needs to be (full re-registration cost × N endpoints × renewal frequency) and increases staleness pressure, since a cheaper renew could run more frequently. Raised by @ravwojdyla in PR #6728 review.

## Proposal

Split renewal from registration: add a cheap, batchable renew path that only carries the `endpoint_id`s (and requested lease duration), so one RPC can renew all of a client's leases at once. The renewer already iterates due leases in `tick`; it could collect them and issue a single batch-renew instead of N register calls.

Sketch:
- New `RenewEndpointLease(s)` RPC taking a list of `endpoint_id`s + a lease duration, returning the granted deadlines (and which ids were not found / expired).
- `EndpointLeaseRenewer.tick` batches all due leases into one call; `_renew_one` per-endpoint retry/backoff bookkeeping folds into a per-batch (or per-id-within-batch) result.
- Keep register-grants-a-lease as-is for the initial registration.

## Notes / priority

Low priority in practice: we typically have ~1 endpoint per task, so the per-renewal cost is small today. Tracking it so it isn't lost once endpoint-per-task counts grow.

Part of #6722. Follow-up from PR #6728.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

HF-format checkpoint export should be a separate `export_hf` `ArtifactStep` that depends on a `LevanterCheckpoint`, instead of an inline callback inside the training run. The inline export is forced on for every run and **cannot succeed on a multi-host TPU**, so multi-host training jobs crash at end-of-training even though training, eval, and the native checkpoint all succeeded.

## How it surfaced

End-to-end validation of the lazy `ArtifactStep` model on `v5litepod-16` (a 4-host v5e gang) ran the full graph correctly — tokenize → Levanter cache → train. Training completed all steps, the held-out eval ran (`eval loss: 9.805`), and the native tensorstore checkpoint was written. The job then failed in the inline HF export:

```
File "lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py", line 1135, in save_pretrained
    shard_numpy = {k: np.asarray(v) for k, v in shard_weights.items()}
File ".../jax/_src/array.py", line 625, in _value
RuntimeError: Fetching value for `jax.Array` that spans non-addressable
(non process local) devices is not possible. You can use
`jax.experimental.multihost_utils.process_allgather` ...
```

One host exited 1; the gang `cosched_failed`; the step wrote no `artifact.json`.

## Root cause

- **Inline HF export runs on the training mesh.** `save_pretrained` materializes each tensor with `np.asarray(global_array)` (`hf_checkpoints.py:1135`). The `reshard(PartitionSpec())` at `:430` replicates a leaf but the replicated **global** array still spans non-addressable devices across hosts, so it is not `is_fully_addressable` and `np.asarray` raises. `max_shard_size` only shards the **output files**, not the device gather. There is no `process_allgather` / `addressable_shards` / `is_fully_addressable` path anywhere in the HF save path — it is an **unconditional multi-host failure**.
- **The native (tensorstore) checkpoint is multi-host-safe** — each process writes its own addressable shards via JAX's GSPMD array serialization — which is why resumption checkpoints survive but the HF export does not.
- **It is forced on with no opt-out.** `bake_output_path` unconditionally sets `hf_save_path = <output_path>/hf` (`training.py:199`), and the trainer runs all hooks with `force=True` at end-of-training (`trainer.py:560,573`), so every run gets a forced final `save_pretrained` regardless of `hf_save_steps`. The `train_lm` API exposes no way to disable it.

## Proposed solution: a separate `export_hf` ArtifactStep

The building blocks already exist and are currently **unwired** (referenced by zero experiments/steps):

- `lib/marin/src/marin/export/levanter_checkpoint.py::convert_checkpoint_to_hf` submits a **separate Fray job** running `levanter.main.export_lm_to_hf`, defaulting to **single-host CPU**, loading the saved **tensorstore** checkpoint into its own mesh and resharding — where every array is fully addressable, so `np.asarray` works.
- `LevanterCheckpoint` (`training.py:56-86`) already exposes `.checkpoint_dir` (the tensorstore root) and `.load`. A downstream `export_hf(checkpoint_handle)` step would declare the train handle as a `dep`, pull `LevanterCheckpoint(path=ctx.artifact_path(train)).checkpoint_dir`, and run `convert_checkpoint_to_hf` on its own right-sized resources. The conversion needs no training devices.

This decouples export from training (training can never again be failed by export), makes the HF artifact independently cacheable and re-runnable, and side-steps the multi-host crash for the common case.

## Two layers of work

1. **Decouple (fixes the crash + the architecture).** Stop forcing inline `hf_save_path` in `bake_output_path`; provide an `export_hf` ArtifactStep wrapping `convert_checkpoint_to_hf`. Small/medium models export on single-host CPU with no levanter change. Migrate experiments that consume `<output_path>/hf` to the step.
2. **"Builtin" multi-host-safe export (for models too large for one host).** A single host cannot hold a giant model, so the export step itself would need a real gather — `process_allgather` / per-host sharded safetensors — which levanter's HF writer lacks today. This is a levanter fix, needed regardless of inline-vs-step.

## Blast radius

Forced inline `<output_path>/hf` is currently produced by **every** training run, so other experiments likely consume it. Removing it from `bake_output_path` is a migration (each consumer adds the `export_hf` step).

## Key references

- `lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:188-200` — `bake_output_path` forces `hf_save_path`
- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py:1135` (`save_pretrained`), `:430` (insufficient reshard), `:1305` (callback)
- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py:560,573` — forced `run_hooks(force=True)` final save
- `lib/marin/src/marin/export/levanter_checkpoint.py` — `convert_checkpoint_to_hf` (unwired building block)
- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/export_lm_to_hf.py` — single-host CPU conversion entry
- `lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:56-86` — `LevanterCheckpoint` (`.checkpoint_dir`, `.load`)

_Filed from an end-to-end validation session for the lazy ArtifactStep / executor-context adoption work._

- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PRs/issues)
- [x] Confirm building blocks + blast radius
- [x] Post approach for review

# Research

Confirmed on `main`. The inline HF export is an unconditional multi-host failure and is forced on with no opt-out:

- `save_pretrained` materializes each shard with `np.asarray(v)` over the **global** array (`hf_checkpoints.py:1135`). The `reshard(PartitionSpec())` at `:430` replicates leaves but the result still spans non-addressable devices across hosts → `np.asarray` raises. `max_shard_size` only shards output files, not the device gather. No `process_allgather`/`is_fully_addressable` path exists.
- It's forced: `bake_output_path` unconditionally sets `hf_save_path=<output_path>/hf` (`training.py:142`); `train_lm` installs the export hook whenever `hf_save_path` is set (`train_lm.py:365-380`); the trainer runs final hooks with `force=True` (`trainer.py:560,573`), so every run does a final `save_pretrained` regardless of `hf_save_steps`. The only opt-out is leaving `hf_save_path=None`.
- Native tensorstore checkpoints are multi-host-safe (per-process addressable shards), which is why resumption survives but HF export doesn't.

**Two corrections to the issue's references** (they're from the in-flight lazy-ArtifactStep branch, not `main`):
- The building block is further along than stated: a full ExecutorStep wrapper **`convert_checkpoint_to_hf_step`** already exists (`export/levanter_checkpoint.py:123-193`), not just `convert_checkpoint_to_hf`. Both are unwired (only re-exported in `export/__init__.py`). It defaults to single-host CPU (`_default_export_resources` = 8 CPU/64g, `:37`) and loads the tensorstore checkpoint into its own mesh where arrays are fully addressable.
- `ArtifactStep`/`LevanterCheckpoint` (issue's `training.py:56-86`) don't exist on `main`; on `main` `training.py:56-86` is `TrainDpoOnPodConfig`. The decouple work layers on top of the executor-context branch.

**Blast radius:** the forced `<output_path>/hf` is consumed downstream — e.g. eval strips it (`evaluation/run.py:139-140`) and ~4 experiments reference `/hf`. Removing it from `bake_output_path` is a migration: each consumer must add the export step.

**Relevant code**
- [`training.py:119-143`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py#L119-L143) — `bake_output_path` forces `hf_save_path`
- [`hf_checkpoints.py:1135`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py#L1135) — `np.asarray` on global array; [`:430`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py#L430) — insufficient reshard
- [`trainer.py:560-573`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L560-L573) — forced final `run_hooks(force=True)`
- [`export/levanter_checkpoint.py:123-193`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/export/levanter_checkpoint.py#L123-L193) — `convert_checkpoint_to_hf_step` (exists, unwired)
- [`evaluation/run.py:139-140`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/run.py#L139-L140) — consumer strips `/hf`

# Proposed approach (for review — not a PR)

Three separable changes; (1) is the actual crash fix and is small, (2)+(3) are the larger migration/levanter work.

1. **Stop forcing inline export.** Drop the `hf_save_path` assignment from `bake_output_path` (and its docstring/`DEFAULT_HF_CHECKPOINTS_PATH` use). This alone unblocks multi-host training — the final forced `save_pretrained` no longer runs. Self-contained, but it removes an artifact every run currently produces, so it can't merge without (2).
2. **Wire `convert_checkpoint_to_hf_step` as the replacement.** The ExecutorStep already exists; add it downstream of training for each consumer of `<output_path>/hf` (depends on the train handle's `checkpoints/` dir, runs on single-host CPU). Migrate the ~4 experiments + eval to consume the step's output instead of `<output_path>/hf`.
3. **(Separate, levanter) multi-host-safe builtin export** for models too big for one host: add `process_allgather`/per-host sharded-safetensors to `save_pretrained`. Needed regardless of inline-vs-step; out of scope for the decouple.

Open questions for a human before implementation:
- Land on top of the executor-context/ArtifactStep branch, or as an independent `ExecutorStep`-based change on `main`? The issue frames it as `ArtifactStep`, which doesn't exist on `main` yet.
- Keep `bake_output_path` setting `hf_save_path` behind an explicit opt-in flag (for single-host runs that want inline export), or remove it entirely and always use the step?

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 Follow-up to the lazy-artifact migration (PR #6649).

## Context

The canary ferry (`experiments/ferries/canary_ferry.py`) and `save_logprobs`
(`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/save_logprobs.py`) both need to **force packing on
every component** of an `LmDataConfig` — the canary because the `gpu_fa4_thd` attention
kernel only handles full causal windows, `save_logprobs` because it always packs.

PR #6649 deduplicated the two copies into one helper,
`marin.processing.tokenize.data_configs.with_pack(data, pack)`, which rewrites every
cache-backed component via `dataclasses.replace`. That removes the duplication but is
still a **post-hoc rewrite** of an already-assembled mixture.

## Why this is still a workaround

Packing is a load-time view, not a cache property: `dataset_for_component`
(`lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py`) wraps the *same* `TreeCache` in a
`PackedTokenDataset` when `pack` is set, else a plain `CausalLmDataset`. So toggling
`pack` never re-tokenizes anything. Packing is applied **per component, before**
`MixtureDataset` combines them by weight — which is correct (packing the mixed stream
would glue documents from different sources into one example and break per-source
weighting/segmentation), so it can't move "to the top" of the dataset graph.

The real gap is config ergonomics. `LmDataConfig.block_cross_document_attention` is a
**top-level field** that fans out to every component at construction. `pack` is the only
one of these cross-cutting knobs with no top-level override — so "pack the whole mixture"
can only be expressed by reaching into `.components` and rewriting each leaf.

## Proposed cleanup

Add a top-level `pack: bool | int | Literal["pad"] | None = None` to `LmDataConfig`
(levanter), symmetric with `block_cross_document_attention`, and apply it as an override
in `dataset_for_component`:

```python
pack = config.pack if config.pack is not None else _effective_pack(component)
```

`None` preserves today's per-component behavior; set it and the whole mixture packs.
Then:

- thread `pack` through `marin.experiment.data.mixture(...)` so the canary becomes
  `mixture(ctx, {slimpajama: 1.0}, pack=1 if thd else None)`;
- `save_logprobs._force_pack_data` collapses to
  `replace(data, pack=True, block_cross_document_attention=True)`;
- delete `with_pack` and its two call sites.

This is a levanter change (one field + one override line + tests), which is why it was
deferred out of the migration PR. Tag with `agent-generated`.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Description
Verify CE path behavior on a fresh readable May profile so we can isolate whether CE contributes to remaining forward/backward bottlenecks.

Parent tracker: #6693

### Definition of Done
- A readable profile for May shape is generated (or existing run is reused).
- B-tiled attribution rows are identified and stable.
- Notes are added on the dominant CE kernels and any practical optimization levers.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Actionability check — clear DoD, but this is a profiling/investigation task (no code defect)
- [x] Locate CE B-tiled path + profiling attribution tooling
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (#5510 is the prior CE investigation)
- [x] Post research + reproducible approach (no PR — needs profiler runs + W&B artifacts I can't access)

# Research

This is a profiling investigation, not a code fix: the DoD is "generate/reuse a readable May profile, identify B-tiled attribution rows, note dominant CE kernels + levers." It needs a live May profile artifact (W&B) and the profiler stack — out of scope for a PR. Below is everything needed to execute it.

The **B-tiled CE path** is the full-vocab batched-XLA forward/backward used on H100. Attribution rows surface through `marin.profiling`, which buckets every CE kernel into the `loss_xent` semantic family via regex on `linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss|softmax_cross_entropy|xent`.

**Relevant code**
- [`batched_xla.py#L317`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/batched_xla.py#L317) — `_linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_full_vocab_b_tiled` (B-tiled forward)
- [`batched_xla.py#L552`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/batched_xla.py#L552) — `_backward_b_tiled_from_lse` (B-tiled backward)
- [`batched_xla.py#L369`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/batched_xla.py#L369) — `_h100_full_vocab_b_tiled_block_size` (selects B-block, e.g. 8192)
- [`semantics.py#L13`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/profiling/semantics.py#L13) — `loss_xent` family regex (the CE attribution bucket)
- [`query.py#L268`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/profiling/query.py#L268) — `_semantic_families_for_summary` (CE exclusive-time rows)

# Proposed approach (for the owner — needs infra)

1. **Get a readable May profile.** Reuse the May215 run referenced in #6693, or take a fresh non-truncated trace. Prior CE work (#5510) repeatedly hit empty `step_time` and trace truncation at 1,000,000 events — verify the reused trace is complete before trusting attribution.

2. **Summarize → CE rows** with the existing CLI (pulls the profiler dir from W&B and aggregates the `loss_xent` family):
   ```bash
   python -m marin.profiling.cli summarize \
     --run-target <may-run-id> --entity marin-community --project marin \
     --breakdown-mode exclusive_per_track --output /tmp/may.json
   python -m marin.profiling.cli query --summary /tmp/may.json \
     --question "loss_xent"   # CE family exclusive time + hot ops
   ```
   The B-tiled rows show up as `linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss` ops; confirm the selected B-block matches `_h100_full_vocab_b_tiled_block_size` and that rows are stable across steps (drop warmup via `--warmup-steps`).

3. **Notes / levers.** Capture CE % of step time and the dominant kernels. Known levers from #5510: XLA streaming is the agreed default (dlwh: "just make xla streaming the default everywhere… for big models it won't be much of a bottleneck"); the H100 native Pallas CE forward does not lower (fp32 LM-head weight tile exceeds the shared-mem guard), and the hybrid XLA-fwd + custom-streaming-bwd gave ~15% CE-only / ~11% tok/s in microbench but no proven end-to-end step-time win.

**Recommendation:** if the May profile shows CE is a small fraction of fwd/bwd time, record that and close the row in #6693 with XLA streaming as the documented default — no native-CE rewrite. Reserve a narrower H100 kernel task only if CE is a measurable bottleneck.

No PR opened — this is investigation work requiring profiler runs and W&B artifacts. Happy to turn any concrete finding into a doc/code change once a profile is available.

comments.body:
🤖 **CE path verified on the May profile — B-tiled rows identified, no fresh run needed (yet).**

Reused three non-truncated `jax_profile:v0` artifacts from `marin-community/marin_moe` (all H100×8, **1 node / 8 devices**, May d2560/L26, 256 experts top-4, S4096, B8/dev, ring MoE, FA4-SGD, vocab 128256, `replica=1`/`expert=8`/`model=1` → pure FSDP + 8-way intra-node expert parallel). The key one is a clean same-day **A/B pair** differing *only* in `model.cross_entropy_implementation`:

- B-tiled: [`...MAY-217...PALLASCEV8192...XENTAB...cw-20260622-0310`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/GM2560-MAY-217S4096-W2048-B8-R1-E8M1-PALLASCEV8192-RING-REPEMB-REPOUT-FA4SGD-XENTAB-N1-cw-20260622-0310) — `cross_entropy_implementation='pallas_gpu'`
- streaming: [`...MAY-217...XLACE...XENTAB...cw-20260622-0310`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/GM2560-MAY-217S4096-W2048-B8-R1-E8M1-XLACE-RING-REPEMB-REPOUT-FA4SGD-XENTAB-N1-cw-20260622-0310) — `cross_entropy_implementation='xla'`

Config diff between the two is exactly one substantive key (`cross_entropy_implementation`), so it's a clean A/B.

## B-tiled path identified (DoD ✓)
- "B-tiled" = `_linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_full_vocab_b_tiled` ([`batched_xla.py#L317`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/batched_xla.py#L317)), gated by `_h100_full_vocab_b_tiled_block_size` (H100 + bf16 + `B≥8192` + `V≥65536` → block **8192**; constants `_H100_FULL_VOCAB_B_TILED_BLOCK_SIZE=8192`, `_H100_FULL_VOCAB_B_TILED_MIN_BATCH=8192`, `_LARGE_VOCAB_THRESHOLD=65536`).
- Impl→run mapping ([`api.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/api.py)): `'xla'`→`linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_xla` (streaming); `'pallas_gpu'`→**renamed to `'batched_xla'`**→`_linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_batched_xla_impl`→on H100 dispatches to `_full_vocab_b_tiled` @ 8192.
- This run qualifies (vocab 128256 ≥ 65536, B≥8192), so **the B-tiled rows live in `MAY-217-PALLASCEV8192`** — the `V8192` in the name is the 8192 B-tile / custom-bwd V-block. Stable across the profiled steps; no trace truncation (247k / 356k events, `suspected_truncation=False`).

## A/B result — B-tiled is the win, not a remaining bottleneck (DoD ✓)
Throughput (W&B summary; **identical loss 11.7933 ⇒ numerically equivalent**):

| metric | XLA streaming | B-tiled @8192 | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| final MFU | 16.34 | 19.12 | **+17.0%** |
| mean MFU | 13.59 | 15.87 | +16.8% |
| tokens/s | 75,570 | 88,430 | +17.0% |
| step time | 0.4336 s | 0.3706 s | −14.5% |

Profile attribution (exclusive device time over the capture window):

| | XLA streaming | B-tiled @8192 | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| device compute | 6107 ms | 5111 ms | −996 ms |
| CE fusions (bucketed in `other`) | 3986 ms / n=35,248 | 3456 ms / n=14,928 | −530 ms / **−20,320 kernels** |

Consistent with the historical A/B in #4312 (CE `1.397s → 0.380s`, −72.8% CE kernel time).

## Dominant CE kernels
CE lowers to many small **unnamed fusion / `_lambda_` kernels** — the LM-head matmul (`[8192×2560×128256]` tiles) plus softmax/logsumexp reductions — bucketed into the `other` family. The streaming path spins **~20k more** of these kernels than b-tiled for identical work; that kernel-count blowup *is* the CE cost, and b-tiled@8192 collapses it.

## Levers / recommendation
- Keep **`batched_xla` (b-tiled @8192)** as the H100 CE default — it's already what the `May402+` baselines run (`PALLASCE`), +17% MFU, numerically identical. For this d2560/B8/vocab-128k shape CE is non-trivial, so "just use XLA streaming everywhere for big models" does **not** apply here.
- After b-tiled, CE is no longer the leading fwd/bwd cost — collectives (ring gather/scatter ~16%) and MoE expert/transport dominate (see #4312). **Recommend closing the CE row** once the reproduction below confirms.

## Tooling gaps found (filing separately)
1. `marin.profiling.cli summarize --run-target <grug run>` fails — grug `marin_moe` runs nest config at `trainer.trainer.log_dir` (resolver expects `trainer.log_dir`) and `log_dir='logs'` is ephemeral on the CW pod. Workaround that works: `summarize --artifact <run>-profiler:v0`.
2. `marin.profiling.semantics` `loss_xent` regex doesn't match GPU CE kernels (unnamed fusions) → CE is invisible as a family on GPU xplane. Needs `jax.named_scope` around the CE/LM-head or shape-based attribution.

## Next: reproduce the A/B
The above reuses existing artifacts; **we will reproduce the pair fresh** to confirm the delta on current `main`, flipping only `model.cross_entropy_implementation` between `batched_xla` (b-tiled@8192) and `xla`. Each run is a single 8×H100 CoreWeave node, ~15 min end-to-end (the science is ~5 s of steps; the rest is node bring-up + compile + 2-step profiler capture). Will post the reproduced numbers here.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Update: reproduced the runs — on current `main`, B-tiled fused CE is silently bypassed in sharded training and is the *slowest* CE arm; one-line policy fix restores it

Correcting my [earlier comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6695) (posted before reproducing) on two points: (1) the CE **per-device batch is 4096**, not `B ≥ 8192` (the +17% A/B there was a June run on the earlier `pallas_gpu` impl); (2) on current `main`, `batched_xla` is **not** the default win — at per-device 4096 it bypasses B-tiled and is slower than `xla`. This fix restores the win.

- **Root cause:** `batched_xla`'s full-vocab B-tiled path only activates at per-call `B ≥ 8192` (the `_H100_FULL_VOCAB_B_TILED_MIN_BATCH` gate, introduced with the current `batched_xla` path in #6572). Training shards the CE 8-way (`loss.py` `shard_map`), so each device sees `32768 / 8 = 4096 < 8192` → fast path bypassed → ~2× slower FA-style streaming fallback.
- **Why the fallback is slow (profile-verified):** it fragments the `[B,H]@[H,V]` LM-head matmul into an unrolled vocab-tile loop — `num_v_blocks = ⌈128256/1024⌉ = 126` small width-`1024` GEMMs (+ backward). In the profiled step the loop body (`loop_dynamic_slice_fusion` = the `w[:, v_start:v_end]` slice, `gemm_fusion_dot_*`, online-softmax `loop_add_fusion`) each fire **32,064×**; non-collective "other" op count is **173,216**.
- **Fix (`63a90b9fc`):** drop the hard batch-minimum; activate on large vocab (`V ≥ 65536`, the real memory driver) and tile by `min(B, 8192)`. Per-device 4096 now runs as one full-vocab GEMM; larger batches still tile to bound peak logits memory. Tests updated; lint + pyrefly clean.
- **Result delta:** training mean MFU **9.51 → 12.6–13.1** (now the fastest CE; `xla` 12.57); "other" op count **173,216 → 14,160**. Standalone microbench at per-device 4096: **−52% → +31%** vs `xla` (the kernel is fine in isolation — reproduces #6596's "GEMM-bound near roofline"; the regression was purely the activation gate vs the sharded batch).
- **Confidence:** replicated (training 3×; standalone gate-sweep 3× at per-device 4096/8192/32768).
- **Ruled out:** `--xla_gpu_triton_gemm_any=false` (fragmentation persists as cuBLAS, MFU flat); missing LM-head sharding (`main` already applies `Plm_head`); jax/jaxlib version (identical 0.10.0).
- **Secondary (single-node MFU after the fix):** reliable ceiling ≈ **14.8 MFU** (b16 / per-device 8192 = max fitting batch; b20/b24/b32 OOM). `--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true` is a real ~+16% lever but adds ~30 GiB peak that only fits reliably at b8 (→14.6); at b16 it OOMs (fit 1 of 4 → NCCL hang; `cuda_malloc_async` no help). The original June ~16 reliably needs a memory/transport change (selective remat, MoE transport #6597, or multi-node), not single-node tuning.

spillover_issues.author: RohithKuditipudi
spillover_issues.body:
## Description
`ResourceConfig.with_tpu([...])` can only express TPU alternatives that share both `vm_count` and `chips_per_vm` (`lib/fray/src/fray/types.py:354`). Iris enforces the same shape constraint when validating `device-variant IN` candidates (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py:720`).

This blocks valid capacity-fallback requests such as "any single-host TPU under 16 chips". Today callers must split that into separate jobs or worker pools:

- `v5litepod-1`, `v6e-1`
- `v4-8`, `v5p-8`, `v5litepod-4`, `v6e-4`
- `v5litepod-8`, `v6e-8`

The limitation is the request encoding: one primary TPU shape plus a `device_variant IN (...)` constraint. A richer resource-union representation could let each candidate carry its own full shape, e.g. `(variant, chips_per_vm, vm_count, replicas)`.

### Definition of Done
- Fray/Iris can represent heterogeneous TPU alternatives without relying on one primary shape.
- Iris validates and schedules each candidate using its own topology.
- Existing same-shape `with_tpu([...])` behavior keeps working.
- Tests cover mixed 1-chip, 4-chip, and 8-chip single-host TPU alternatives.
